en: Commentary on the *Saptakoṭi-Buddhamātṛ-Sūtra-Spoken-Cundī-Dhāraṇī*, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of Central India, the Great Sage Amoghavajra, by Imperial Decree during the Tang Dynasty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Hongzan of Bodhicitta at Mount Dinghu in Qingyue, East China.
According to the teachings of the Tathāgata throughout his lifetime, the doctrine is divided into the Three Piṭakas, namely: Sūtra, Vinaya, and [Abhidharma].
*Sūtra* refers to the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras. Although the Pitakas are divided into three, they do not transcend the two gates of Exoteric and Esoteric.
The Exoteric extensively discusses *dharmatā* (nature) and *lakṣaṇa* (characteristics), bringing about awakening to profound principles and the cultivation and realization of the *dharmakāya*.

The Esoteric, however, merely requires recitation and retention without the addition of analytical understanding, whereby one silently ascends to the ranks of the sages. Nevertheless, there are sudden and gradual modes of awakening, and levels of rank that vary in depth. Regarding the gradual...

Thus, one may pass through various *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, or suddenly and directly transcend the ten stages (*bhūmi*). At the shallow level, there is the enlightenment of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*;
at the profound level, there is the realization of the Mahāyāna Buddha-fruit. This present Cundī Dhāraṇī is precisely the esoteric teaching within the Sūtra-piṭaka;

it is the silent realization of the Mahāyāna Buddha-fruit of the ten bodies (*daśakāya*). Alternatively, apart from the Three Piṭakas, one may establish a separate "Miscellaneous Piṭaka" (*Kṣudraka-piṭaka*).
The various *dhāraṇīs* are collected [herein]. Alternatively, outside of the Three Vehicles, the supreme Vajrayāna is established separately;

this is precisely the *dhāraṇī-piṭaka*. According to the *Shenbian shu* (Commentary on the Divine Transformations), *dhāraṇīs* are categorized as the Great Inconceivable Vehicle of the Spiritual Powers for Attaining Buddhahood.
Therefore, this sutra takes the great secret as its primary tenet: the *tathatā* of the *dharmadhātu*.
Its essence is the inconceivable; its function is the inconceivable; its gate is the three mysteries; and its doctrinal characteristic is the Supreme Vehicle.
This is because all dharmas flow forth from within the Vajra Dhāraṇī Vehicle, just as thousands of streams and ten thousand tributaries originate from Mount Kunlun and the Stone Shingle Pass.
Thus, the Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of the teachings emerge from the secret treasury of total retention (*dhāraṇī*).
The treasury [of all dharmas], including even the six perfections and the myriad practices, all emerge from this *dhāraṇī*.

This means that each and every syllable of the mantra is entirely the signless *dharmadhātu*, and thus there are no six perfections or myriad practices that do not flow forth from within this *dharmadhātu*.
Therefore, it is said: "The syllable *Oṃ* signifies the three bodies (*trikāya*), and is also the primordial basis of all phenomena."
Regarding the meaning of "arising": because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, one attains non-arising and non-ceasing.
Because of this non-arising and non-ceasing, one attains the non-apprehension of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). This non-apprehension of characteristics is the signless *dharmadhātu*.

In reality, this is the realization of the *tathatā* of the *dharmadhātu*. Therefore, the *Śvetāśvatara-parivarta* (White Parasol Sūtra) states: "Recite [the mantra] eighteen thousand times. Each recitation...
He entered the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*) and was named Sovereign of the Firm Vajra Banner (*Sthira-vajra-dhvaja-īśvara*).
He attained the title of Buddha among Men (*puruṣa-buddha*). Furthermore, the *Pañca-guhya-sādhana-vidhi* states: "Vajrasattva is Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
he is the eldest son of all Tathāgatas and the bodhicitta of all Tathāgatas," as it is said in the sūtra.
It is said: "The samādhi of Vajrasattva is called the Dharma of all Buddhas. This Dharma can accomplish the path of all Buddhas;
apart from this Dharma, there is nothing else that can lead to Buddhahood. Those who wish to know the Vajra should know it is named Prajñāpāramitā.
It penetrates all Buddhas without stagnation or obstruction, just like gold."

It is firm. For this reason, it gives birth to all Buddhas. If one practices according to the teachings of manifestation (*vyākhyāna-dharma*), one must pass through three great incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) before finally realizing unsurpassed bodhi. During that interval, there are nine retreats for every ten advances;
or one may realize the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), yet with the merit and wisdom thus accumulated, one dedicates them toward the fruits of the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Nevertheless...
One cannot realize unsurpassed bodhi. However, if one relies upon the Dharma of the internally realized, self-awakened noble wisdom,
as well as the stage of the Great Samantabhadra Vajrasattva, and the wisdom of the saṃbhogakāya—
up to its timely accumulation within the body through the merit accumulated over one great asaṃkhyeya kalpa— as taught by the *svasaṃbhogakāya* of Vairocana Buddha, [one may attain it].
Possessing virtue and wisdom, they are thereby born into the family of the Buddhas.

Such persons are born from the mind of all Tathāgatas, born from the mouth of the Buddha, born from the Buddha-Dharma, and born through transformation by the Dharma; they obtain the wealth of the Buddha-Dharma. From this point forward...
Having received the vast, profound, and inconceivable Dharma, one transcends the two vehicles and the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
It is known that the secret purport of the mantras is not even accessible to Bodhisattvas at the stage of cause; how much less could it be fathomed by the limited intelligence of ordinary people?
Therefore, this assembly of translators, together with various commentaries and sub-commentaries, has briefly elucidated them in mutual clarification for the benefit of beginners.
I have studied and recited this, and though I have applied my mind to it, I dare not claim to have explained it.
As the *Commentary on the Manifestation of the Divine Powers* (*Shenbian shu*) states: "Only Vajrapāṇi may probe its jaw; only Padmanetra can peer into its depths. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"The secret Dharma of all Buddhas is understood only by Buddha and Buddha themselves; it is not something that other sages can fully penetrate."
Simply maintain its recitation; it can extinguish great transgressions and enable one to swiftly ascend to the rank of a sage. The *Tianzhu Zhiguan* states:

"Only those of the highest sages are capable of expounding both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings. Ordinary people can only propagate the Exoteric teachings and cannot propagate the Esoteric teachings;
therefore, this is not a matter for discussion by those of inferior capacity. This can be understood through the teacher’s own mind. Now, according to this *Cundī Dhāraṇī*: [the preceding...]
Thereafter, it was translated several times. However, the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra deeply attained the transmission of the Esoteric Teachings;
for in the past, Vajrasattva personally received the meaning of the Yoga Supreme Vehicle before the Tathāgata Vairocana-Muni.
Several hundred years later, it was transmitted to Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna. Another several hundred years later, it was transmitted to Ācārya Nāgabodhi.

Nāgabodhi transmitted it to Dharma Master Vajrabodhi. When Vajrabodhi came to travel in China (Zhendan), he bestowed the five classes of Yoga, as well as the *Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi-sūtra* and the *Susiddhikara-vidhi*, upon Amoghavajra.

When Kūkai and his fellow Tripitaka masters entered nirvana, the Tripitaka masters followed their final instructions and traveled again through various kingdoms of India to further expand their learning.

In the Kingdom of Siṃhala, they sought from the Ācārya Nāgabodhi the opening of the eighteen assemblies of the Vajra-Abhiṣeka and the Dharma of the Great Compassion Womb (Mahākaruṇā-garbha). This transmission of the Dharma has been passed down from Vairocana...
As for that Tathāgata, he reached the Venerable Amoghavajra after six generations.

Since Amoghavajra traveled extensively throughout India and further obtained the personally transmitted precepts, the *mantra* texts and ritual manuals he translated are exhaustive, detailed, and complete.

Now, fearing that beginners may not yet be familiar with Sanskrit sounds and mudrās, I have, among all available translations, largely adopted the version translated by Jñānagupta to clarify this work.
This is because it has been transmitted through a succession of teachers and disciples, handed down without interruption.
Thus have I heard.
This means that the Tathāgata, according to the principle of reality as it truly is, preached this method of the Cundī Dhāraṇī; therefore, it is said "Thus.
Venerable Ānanda personally heard such a teaching from the Buddha; therefore, it is said "I have heard."
At one time. This refers to the time when this sutra was spoken. The Bhagavan.
This is the designation for the Tathāgata’s supreme and ultimate multitude of virtues. It possesses six meanings: first, mastery; second, brilliance;
third, physical excellence; fourth, renown; fifth, auspiciousness; and sixth, nobility. These are explained in detail elsewhere.
In the city named Mahānāman,
known in the language of Brahmā as Śrāvastī,
is the Jetavana Grove.
The old translation says "Jeta’s Tree" (*Jetavana*), meaning that the grove of trees was bestowed by Prince Jeta.
As for "Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden," Anāthapiṇḍada is an alternative name for the elder Sudatta; the garden was purchased by the elder with the distribution of gold.
This is the place where the two [disciples] together offered their gifts; thus it is called by this collective name.
He was surrounded before and behind by a great assembly of bhikṣus, as well as by various bodhisattvas and the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas.
This is the assembly listening to the Dharma.
Out of compassion for sentient beings of the future who possess meager merit and commit evil deeds,
he immediately entered the Cundī Samādhi and spoke the dhāraṇī taught by seven hundred million buddhas of the past, saying:
"Compassionate mindfulness" (minkian) means that the Tathāgata regards sentient beings with pity and loving-kindness. In Sanskrit, *samādhi*; in Chinese, "equanimous maintenance" (dengchi).
This refers to that which maintains the equilibrium of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). *Koṭi* means "one hundred billion" in Chinese.
*Dhāraṇī* means "total retention" (zongchi) in Chinese; it refers to the total retention of all dharma-gates, encompassing inexhaustible teachings, principles, practices, and realizations.
It is a fruit. Furthermore, it maintains the good so that it is not lost and maintains the evil so that it does not arise;

thus, it is also translated as "obstructing and maintaining" (*zhe-chi*), meaning to obstruct the evils of the two extremes and maintain the goodness of the Middle Way. Its specific name, "mantra" (*zhòu*), is not a direct translation.
Since it contains many meanings, it cannot be fully explained by conventional terminology. To investigate its reality, it is none other than Vairocana Tathāgata.
This is the Great Inconceivable Secret Heart-Seal of all Buddhas. Namo saptānāṃ samyaksaṃbuddhakoṭīnām | Tadyathā | Oṃ care cule cuṇe svāhā ||
(8) Whenever reciting a mantra, the syllable *oṃ* should be drawn out. The phrases must be distinct; the tone should be neither too slow nor too hurried.
This will be explained in detail below.
This mantra consists of eight phrases. The first three phrases are words of homage and respect to the Buddhas, serving as the introduction to the spell.
The following five phrases constitute the actual body of the mantra. Regarding the term "protracted" (āyati), it means to draw out the sound for a long duration.
Regarding "combined" (saṃyukta), it means that two syllables are merged into a single sound. Vajrajñāna translated this as *jvale jvāle candre svāhā*. Its...
The character "shàng" (上) has a mouth radical on its side; the character "nán" (南) likewise has a mouth radical on its side.
In the *lì* (隸) script, these are pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*). *Dīpāhara* translates it as: *zhé lì zhǔ lì zhǔn dì suō pó hē*.
*Jñānagupta* translates it as: *zhé lì zhǔ lì zhǔn dì suō hē*. *Devaśānti* translates it as: *Namo sabodhanam*. Three.
*Namo bhagavate guhyakādhipataye*. Tadyathā: Oṃ cale cule cuṇḍe svāhā. (The character *mo* is pronounced with an entering tone;
*pat* is a double-syllable; *tha* is pronounced with a departing tone; the character *oṃ* and both instances of *li* are drawn out [protracted];
*cuṇ* is pronounced with an ascending tone; *ḍe* is drawn out; the remainder is as above). Translated by Faxian.
In the *Mahāsāmghika* and *Devīparitrāṇa*, the first phrases are identical in all cases. In the second phrase, the three characters [ending with] *kṣi* are a conjunct (*dvirukta*).
The characters *tso* (祖) and *tsun* (尊) lack the vowel *u*. There are various differences among these translations because the Indic sounds undergo shifts in weight;
thus, the characters are not uniform. However, since these are Indic sounds, one should adopt the sound of the character rather than its semantic meaning. If it were...
Regarding those who are skilled in the *brahmasvara* (Sanskrit pronunciation): when reciting the various translations mentioned above, there is no difference;
one may choose any single translation to recite. Provided that the *brahmasvara* is not corrupted, all are acceptable.

As for those characters with the "mouth-side" (*kha-ṅa*) vowel, one must curl the tongue to pronounce them, and thus the correct sound will be attained. *Namo*, sometimes written as *nama*, sometimes as *namo*, or sometimes as *nan*.
"Na-mo" means "to take refuge" in the language of China; it is also called "taking refuge" (*pratiśaraṇa*).
"Tadyathā" means "as follows" in the language of China, and is also said to mean "now I shall speak. "Svāhā" is translated as "accomplishment";
it also signifies "auspiciousness," "parinirvāṇa," "the dispelling of calamities and the increase of merit," or "non-abiding. This refers to non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*).
Because there will be no end to the benefit of sentient beings throughout the limits of the future,
if any bodhisattvas— whether ordained or lay— who practice the way of mantra recite and uphold this dhāraṇī ninety thousand times,
then the ten evil deeds, the five heinous crimes, the four grave offenses, and the five sins of immediate retribution committed over immeasurable kalpas shall all be entirely [purified].

They shall be extinguished. In whatever place they are born, they will always encounter Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, possess abundant wealth and treasures, and will always be able to leave the household life.
As for the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*), they are: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, frivolous speech, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, greed, anger, and wrong views.
The "four grave offenses" refer to the violation of the four prohibitions: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying. The "five heinous crimes" are: first, patricide; second, matricide;
third, shedding the blood of a Buddha; fourth, killing an Arhat; and fifth, causing a schism in the Saṃgha.

If one commits even a single such crime, one immediately falls into the Avīci Hell and suffers there for one kalpa. One who has committed all five is thus described [as having committed the five heinous crimes].

The five crimes of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*). In Sanskrit, this is *avīci*; here it is translated as "uninterrupted. This means that once one has fallen into this hell, one suffers for a full great kalpa (*mahākalpa*) without even a moment's respite, such as the snapping of a finger.

If a lay bodhisattva practices the precepts with firm resolve and without regression, and recites this dhāraṇī, they will always be reborn in the celestial realms or among humans as a king, never falling into the evil destinies. They will draw near to the worthy and holy ones, be loved and respected by the devas, and receive their protection and empowerment.
Should they attend to worldly affairs, they will be free from calamities and misfortunes; their appearance will be upright and handsome, and their speech...

The sound is majestic and awe-inspiring; the mind is free from sorrow and affliction. If an ordained bodhisattva maintains all the prohibitive precepts, recites the mantras at the three times of day, and practices according to the teachings, then the supramundane *siddhi* sought in this present life will be attained, concentration and wisdom will manifest before them, they will realize the perfection of the stages (*bhūmi-pāramitā*), and they will swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
A lay bodhisattva upholds the five precepts, the ten wholesome actions, and the bodhisattva mahāśīla; therefore, it is said that they "cultivate and maintain the practice of ethical discipline.
A renunciant bodhisattva upholds both the śrāmaṇera and bhikṣu vinaya, as well as the bodhisattva prātimokṣa; therefore, it is said that...

To possess all the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*). "Supramundane *siddhi*" refers to the manifestation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), culminating in the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
*Siddhi* here means "accomplishment" (*cheng*); it signifies the fulfillment of the great aspirations sought in both the mundane and supramundane realms.
Because it encompasses many meanings, there is no direct equivalent translation. Regarding the term "realizing the stages" (*zhengdi*), this explains the [meaning of] *bhūmi*.

The *Luoṇi* (Dhāraṇī) states: Within the *Yogācāra*, from the stage of ordinary beings to that of the sages, there are four stages in total. First, the Stage of Practice through Resolute Belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), which generally refers to the stages prior to the [ten] bhūmis.

Second, the Stage of Samantabhadra’s Vows and Practices (*samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna-bhūmi*), which generally refers to the ten bhūmis. Third, the Great Stage of Samantabhadra (*mahā-samantabhadra-bhūmi*).
This is the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-bhūmi*). Fourth is the stage of Universal Radiance (*samantaprabhā-bhūmi*), which is the stage of attaining Perfect Enlightenment;
it is also called the stage of the universal light of the three bodies of Vairocana. Regarding the *pāramitās*, they refer to the six *pāramitās* as well as the ten *pāramitās*.
The *Mahāyāna-ratnarāja-sūtra* and other scriptures state that practitioners who maintain and recite the mantra practices shall daily attain [these perfections].

Because of the merit of fulfilling the six *pāramitās*, various *dhāraṇī* sūtras state that practitioners of the mantra path can achieve unsurpassed *bodhi* in the present life. The *Five-Syllable Dhāraṇī Verse* says:
"By the power of the original vows of all Buddhas, one accomplishes all holy deeds in the present; even within a single sitting, one attains supreme perfect enlightenment."
If one recites it ten thousand times—
according to the translation by Zhi, this refers to one hundred thousand times—
one will see the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in a dream and immediately vomit out black matter.
The black substance represents evil karma; its immediate expulsion is a sign that sin is being extinguished and merit is arising.
Therefore, one sees for oneself a black substance being spat out from the mouth, or what some call "black rice."
If that person’s transgressions are particularly grave, they should recite it twenty thousand times—
other translations state twenty thousand times [is equivalent to] two hundred thousand times— and they will likewise see black rice being spat out from their own mouth.
That is, one sees various celestial palaces and monasteries in a dream; or one ascends a high mountain, or sees oneself climbing a tree.
Because one is not burdened by sinful karma, one is able to ascend and tread upon them. Because one has accomplished virtuous causes, one thus sees the celestial palaces and monasteries.
Or they bathe in a great pool to wash away the defilements of their sins, thereby attaining a pure body;
or they see themselves soaring through the air.
Because they are not entangled by sinful karma, their bodies move with lightness.
Or, they may see themselves sporting with various celestial maidens;
this is because they are in accord with the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness, and thus they see themselves sporting with them.
In some cases, they see him preaching the Dharma,
thereby providing instruction, benefit, and joy;
in other cases, they see him plucking out his hair or shaving it off.

Plucking out the hair is the practice of non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika) in the western regions. Plucking out the hair or shaving the head both symbolize the severing of the roots of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Zhi’s translation states: "Or one sees [the practitioner] plucking out their hair or shaving their own head."
Some eat curd-rice and drink white nectar;
eating curd-rice signifies the accomplishment of worldly merit and goodness, while drinking nectar refers to attaining the flavor of the supramundane Dharma.
Or crossing over great oceans and rivers,
they attain the transcendence of the sea of suffering;
or ascending the lion throne.
That is to say, attaining the seat of the Dharma King,
or seeing the Bodhi tree—
these are the signs of the Path of Seeing.
Or one may see oneself riding in a boat;
this is the sign of boarding the Prajñā-boat to reach the further shore. The Susiddhikara Sūtra states:
"Or seeing oneself riding upon a lion, elephant, ox, deer, goose, or the like, these are all signs of the accomplishment of siddhi."
Some see śramaṇas who,
having attained freedom from worldly defilements, have emerged from the three realms;
others see householders with their heads covered by white or yellow garments.
"Yellow for the outer surface and white for the inner surface. This means that one should cover and protect it with a cloth of pure white dharma;
the *Zhì* (智) commentary explains this as covering the head with a garment.
Or one may see the sun and moon,
which symbolize the shattering of the darkness of ignorance and afflictions;
or one may see young boys and girls.
They are not defiled by the afflictions of greed and desire.
Alternatively, there may be milk-yielding fruit trees above;
"milk" signifies whiteness, and whiteness signifies wholesome karma—that is, the attainment of the karmic fruits and retributions of both mundane and supramundane wholesome deeds.
Or one may see a black man from whose mouth flames issue; by fighting him and emerging victorious, it means that one has triumphed in battle against the Māra of the affliction of hatred.
Or one may see a vicious horse or a water buffalo about to charge; the reciter strikes it or rebukes it, causing it to flee in terror.
"Departure" means attaining victory over the māra of the affliction of delusion; alternatively,
it refers to consuming milk porridge or curd-rice.
This refers to attaining the accomplishment of meritorious goodness through superior flavors;
or it is seeing the *sumana* flower—
so called because its name means "pleasing to the mind"— which is yellowish-white in color and extremely fragrant, with a tree height of three or four feet that hangs downward like...
"Covering" (gai) means that the virtuous dharmas sought will certainly be attained as desired. Master Zhi translates it as: "Alternatively, one may see fragrant white flowers.
Fragrance symbolizes the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body, meaning that one attains the fivefold wholesome karma.
Or one may see a king, which signifies that one has received the protective mindfulness of a Great Being and has attained noble and superior karma.
If one does not see such visions, it should be known that this person committed the five crimes of immediate retribution in a previous life. One ought to...

If one further recites it seventy thousand times until completion, one will immediately see the aforementioned visions; one should know that the transgressions have been extinguished and that the preliminary practice has been accomplished.
This requires reciting seventy thousand times; the previous mention of ten thousand or twenty thousand is an error and should be understood as being like the other two cases.
Translated as: one hundred thousand or two hundred thousand [recitations] shall suffice.
The realms seen in dreams as described above are all signs of the practitioner’s realization and accomplishment. The Susiddhi Tantra states: "In that dream, one sees the Lord of Mantras."
He turns his back and departs, or does not speak with one. In such cases, one must once again begin the recitation from the start. This should be done two or three times.
If, within a dream, one sees the Lord of Mantras speaking with them, it should be known that this person will achieve accomplishment before long.
If no such sign occurs, one should not continue the recitation; if one forces oneself to recite, there is fear that it may bring misfortune upon others. At the time of first beginning the recitation:

Begin at a pure and secret place, and then draw the original image according to the ritual (namely, the image of the Honored One Tārā). Whether three times, four times, or six times a day, perform the offerings according to the ritual to seek mundane and supramundane *siddhis*, up to and including unsurpassed *bodhi*; all shall be attained.

It is so. If there are those who practice and uphold this dhāraṇī, one should know that regarding their future places of accomplishment—whether they will encounter obstacles or not, and whether their *siddhi* will be swift or slow—they should prepare a small altar in a clean room, smeared with cow dung (*gomaya*).

According to their means, they should make offerings and bind the boundaries of the ten directions (the four cardinal points, the four intermediate directions, above, and below) using the boundary-binding mantra (*sīmābandha-mantra*). They should then place a flask of scented water upon it.
Within the maṇḍala, recite the mantra with single-minded concentration. If the flask moves or turns, one should know that the matter at hand and the sought-after objective will be accomplished;
if it does not move or turn, the matter will not be achieved.

The mantra for binding the boundary (*sīmā-bandhana*). As follows, it is extracted from the *Dharaṇīśvararāja-sūtra* and other texts concerning the binding of the earth boundary (*bhūmi-sīmā*) and the wall boundary (*prākāra-sīmā*).

The translation by Jñānagupta states: "If, before an image of the Buddha, or before a stūpa, or in a pure place, one smears the ground with *gomaya* (cow dung) and constructs a square altar measuring four cubits (*hasta*), and further prepares, according to one's means, incense, flowers, banners, canopies, food and drink, lamps, and candles."

Perform the offerings according to the ritual. If you wish to seek a specific aspiration, you must first perform recitation and empower scented water, which is then sprinkled in the eight directions and above and below to establish the boundary (*sīmābandha*).
Once the boundary has been established, place a vase of scented water at each of the four corners of the altar and one in its center.
The practitioner faces east and kneels with legs crossed, reciting [the mantra] one thousand and eighty times.
The vases will then turn of their own accord, moving freely to the east or west and ascending or descending at will. *Héluó* (訶羅) translates as:

"Recite mantras over scented water and scatter it in the four directions, above, and below to establish a boundary. Place one scented water vase at each of the four corners and the center of the altar.
The mantra-holder, positioned within the altar facing east, kneels on his right knee and recites [the mantra].
Recite the mantra one thousand and eighty times. Regarding what is called "empowering scented water": one should recite the root mantra twenty-one times and sprinkle it in the ten directions.
Furthermore, according to another method: take a ceramic bowl, smear it with incense, place it within the mandala, and recite with single-minded concentration; if the bowl begins to rotate...
If it moves, the matter will be accomplished; if it does not move, the matter will not be accomplished.
The Zhi translation states: "Using a clean earthen bowl, fumigate it with incense, apply fragrant ointments to both its interior and exterior, and fill it to the brim with scented water."
Together with fine incense and flowers, place them within the maṇḍala and perform the recitation according to the previous method for the flask (*kalaśa*).

The bowl will then rotate, no different from the flask. If you wish to know whether all matters will be accomplished or not, burn incense and address the Noble One, praying that he resolve your doubts:
"If it rotates to the right, there will be accomplishment; if it rotates to the left, then..."
It is not accomplished.
Furthermore, there is another method. If one wishes to know future events, first smear a small mandala.
Have a youth of auspicious marks and merit bathe and purify himself, dress him in new, clean clothes, and smear [the mandala] with incense empowered by seven *koṭi* recitations of the mantra.
The youth’s hand. Furthermore, empower a flower seven times and place it in the youth’s hand; have the youth cover his face and stand within the mandala.
Then, take another flower, empower it by reciting the mantra, and strike the back of the youth’s hand once for each recitation.
Up to twenty-one beads, one should ask the youth about matters of good and evil; the youth will explain them all.
[The master] instructs the translator to take beautiful flowers, recite the mantra one hundred and eight times, and smear the powder of incense upon the youth’s hands.
Holding a flower to cover her face, she again takes another flower with her own hand and, while reciting the mantra, hurls it at the body of the youth.
Furthermore, there is another method: take a bright mirror and place it within the mandala. First, recite the mantra over the flower one hundred and eight times to empower it;
thereafter, recite the mantra once for each throw, striking the surface of the mirror. Upon the surface of the mirror, immediately...
There appear written characters that explain matters of good and evil.
Translated by Jñāna. Alternatively, the messenger manifests directly within the mirror; this messenger is the messenger of the Buddha-mother.

Furthermore, there is another method. If one wishes to know whether a matter is auspicious or inauspicious, and whether it will be accomplished or not, one should take *sumana* flower oil and empower it by reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Anointing the surface of the right thumb with this oil, one should recite the mantra with an uninterrupted voice while having a youth observe the surface of the thumb;
there, the forms of various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or [the form of] a *vidyādhara*, will appear.
[The character] "zi" (mark/sign). To explain fully [the method for] good and evil:
the translation by Zhi states that one may use vermilion or *sumana* flowers, soak them in sesame oil, and smear it on the thumbnail.
Reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, the celestial deities, as well as the Saṅgha, Bodhisattvas, Buddhas, and so forth, will immediately appear.
Regarding the image: if one has doubts concerning matters of the three periods of time, one may ask about each one and know them all; they will then appear spontaneously upon the thumb.

Furthermore, there is another method: if a person suffers from a disease caused by malevolent spirits, take a branch of willow or a blade of sacrificial grass, recite the mantra, and brush over the afflicted area.
The person’s body will immediately be healed. *Héluó* (訶羅) translates this as:
"Recite the mantra over *kuśa* grass and sweep the patient with it. *Gandha-kuśa* (fragrant *kuśa*) is best; if that is unavailable, ordinary *kuśa* grass will also suffice.
*Zhì* (智) translates this as: "Using branches of pomegranate, white *kuśa* incense, and other such herbs, recite the mantra while lashing and sweeping [the patient]."
Furthermore, there is another method: if one suffers from a grave illness, recite the mantra one hundred and eight times while calling the person's name by name;
perform a homa offering with cow’s milk, and the illness will be cured immediately.
This refers to taking *kuśa* grass and other materials, kneading them with milk, reciting mantras while performing the ritual, and casting them into fire to burn; this is called *homa*.
The Chinese translation states: "Place *kuśa* grass in clarified butter (*ghṛta*), recite [the mantra] seven times, and cast it into the fire to burn it.
By letting the smoke from this fumigate the patient, they will be cured. As for what is called "clarified butter," it refers to cow's milk that has been churned and refined.

From curd, butter is produced; from butter, fresh butter (*navanīta*) is produced; from fresh butter, clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is produced; and from clarified butter, the finest essence (*sarpis*) is produced.
Furthermore, according to another method: if a child cries at night, have a young girl twist a thread with her right hand, empower it by reciting the mantra, and tie twenty-one knots.
Fasten it beneath the child’s neck, and the child will immediately cease crying at night.
Other translations state: Have a young girl combine threads of five colors; for each mantra recited, tie a knot until twenty-one knots are complete.
Give these to the patient, or tie them around the necks of small boys or girls; then diseases caused by evil spirits, demons, and malevolent ghosts will be immediately cured.
Furthermore, there is another method. First, empower white mustard seeds one hundred and eight times.

Then, taking the mustard seeds, recite the mantra once for each seed as you cast them to strike the possessing spirit. When this is completed twenty-one times, that spirit will flee and the patient will be cured.
The Chinese translation states: Alternatively, place white mustard seeds in clarified butter. Taking a small amount of the seeds, recite the mantra once and cast one seed into the fire.
Do this twenty-one times, and the illness will be immediately cured.

Furthermore, there is another method. For those afflicted by malevolent spirits (*bhūta-graha*), one should smear a small altar with cow dung and draw the form of the spirit upon the ground using flour-charcoal.
While reciting the mantra, one should lash it with a staff made of pomegranate wood or similar materials; the spirit will then weep and flee away.
Translated by Zhi. The ritual procedure is the same as this. Translated by He Luo: one should have the form of the patient drawn with ink before the sick person;
by reciting the mantra over a willow branch and striking this drawn figure, the illness may likewise be cured. *Gomaya* means "cow dung" in this language.

Furthermore, there is another method. If a person is possessed by a malevolent spirit (*bhūta*), or if the sick person is in a distant location and cannot come in person, or if the practitioner reciting the mantra cannot go to that place, one should take a willow branch, a peach branch, or a flower, empower it one hundred and eight times, and have someone carry it to the patient’s location.
One should then brush the patient with the branch or use the flower.
The patient smells it, or strikes the patient with the flower; the malevolent spirit immediately departs and the patient is cured.
The *Zhìyì* (Jñānagupta) translation says: "Send someone to take it and say to that spirit: 'Go! So-and-so has sent this branch to lash you.
If you do not go, there is no doubt you will be harmed. If they do not leave, lash them and they will depart."
Furthermore, there is another method: if one is bitten by a snake or possessed by a *nāginī* female spirit, one should circumambulate the patient while reciting the mantra;
the illness will then be cured immediately.
That is to say, if one circumambulates and recites [the mantra] around a patient several times, they will immediately recover.
Furthermore, there is another method: if a person suffers from boils, swellings, or the bites of various venomous insects, one should take sandalwood juice mixed with earth to form a paste;
after reciting the mantra seven times, apply it to the wound, and it will immediately heal.

According to the translation by Zhi, one should take the incense of Xunmu, mix it with pure water and soil, and apply it to warts, sores, carbuncles, ringworm, or discharges; these will be healed immediately.
Furthermore, there is another method: if a person is traveling on a road and recites this mantra, they will not be robbed or harmed by bandits, nor will they encounter other calamities.
Regarding the hardships caused by wicked birds, beasts, and the like:

the *Zhì* (Jñāna) translation states that if one travels at night on the road, provided there is no deficiency in one's recitation, there will be no fear or danger from thieves, robbers, tigers, wolves, malevolent spirits, or other such perilous places.
By maintaining the mind in recitation and performing the protection of the body, all such hardships shall immediately [cease].

All shall perish by themselves. When begging for alms, if one constantly maintains this mantra, one will not be harmed by wicked people, malicious dogs, or similar creatures; alms will be easily obtained.
Furthermore, there is another method: if one is engaged in strife, litigation, legal disputes, or debates seeking victory, one should recite this mantra. It brings about powerful triumph;
the Cundī mantra is like a vajra—when aimed at anything, it shatters it all, and none dare withstand it. Therefore, regarding disputes...
Regarding the theory of litigation: in discussing and explaining names, phrases, dharmas, and meanings, one shall be victorious in all cases.

Furthermore, according to the Dharma: if one travels upon rivers or streams and recites this mantra, one shall not be swept away or drowned, nor shall one be harmed by evil dragons, makaras, tortoises, crocodiles, or the like within the water.
*Makara*—this is translated as "whale"; it is over ten *li* long, or perhaps several hundred *li*, and is capable of swallowing large ships.

"And so forth" refers to various venomous insects and snakes. The Zhi translation states: "If bitten by a snake, one immediately dispatches those people to circumambulate [the victim] while reciting the mantra; the person will then be healed."
Furthermore, there is another method: if one is imprisoned or confined, by reciting this dhāraṇī, one will swiftly attain liberation.
Because the essence of the bodhicitta is empty by its very nature, it is free from all things; like the nature of a lotus, it cannot be defiled.
Since this dhāraṇī flows forth from the bodhicitta of all Buddhas, the practitioner who upholds and recites it—self-...
Yet one will swiftly attain liberation.
Furthermore, there is another method: if there is an epidemic within a country, perform *homa* for ten nights using sesame seeds, non-glutinous rice, clarified butter, and honey;
the calamity will then be extinguished, and the land will become peaceful and secure.

The translation by Zhi states: "If in a land the waters and droughts are not regulated, and pestilence spreads among cattle, horses, and other livestock, one should take sesame, barley, non-glutinous rice, millet, beans, ghee, honey, milk, curd, white-milk wood, and various incenses, and set them all aside.
Then, burning incense and making a vow, one should act for the sake of all sentient beings to eliminate disasters and calamities."
Then, forming hand-seals (*mudrā*) and performing recitation (*japa*) for self-protection, take the aforementioned items and empower them through recitation before casting them into the fire to burn.
Perform this rite three times daily for seven days, reciting one thousand and eighty times at each session.
Thereby, one’s wishes will be fulfilled, all shall be peaceful and happy, and all the Triple Gem will provide protection and mindfulness; furthermore, one will also be able to...
This accomplishes all great vows. *Hara* translates as "one should mix ghee with sesame and non-glutinous rice;
taking a pinch with three fingers, recite the mantra once and cast it into the fire to burn.

Whether for seven days and nights, or throughout the six periods of the day and night, if one continues this in succession without interruption, no calamities or epidemics will fail to be extinguished. Thus it is said.
Regarding "hand-seals" (mudrā): this refers to forming mudrās with the hands.

Furthermore, according to the ritual method, if one seeks abundant wealth and treasures, by performing homa with various kinds of food every day, one will immediately obtain an abundance of wealth and treasures.
The *Zhì* (智) translation states: "If one seeks wealth and abundance, place non-glutinous rice and sesame seeds in clarified butter and curd.

Holding a small amount in the hand, make a vow and recite the mantra seven times, then cast it into the fire to burn. Do this according to one's ability for seven days, or even up to forty-nine days, and it will be fulfilled according to one's wish.
The *Héluó* (訶羅) translation states: "Mix clarified butter with rice grains and recite the mantra one hundred times."
Eight times. Burn it within the fire. Whatever one’s heart desires shall be truly accomplished; wealth and treasures will increase and overflow.
As for what is called *homa*, it refers to casting the aforementioned substances into the fire and burning them as an offering.
The Susiddhi Tantra states: "In front of the honored image, construct a *homa* hearth, one cubit square at the top, with four..."
The rim should be placed securely; its depth is half an elbow, and its height is four finger-widths. It should be smeared with a mixture of cow dung and cow urine and sprinkled with scented water.
Alternatively, one may construct a circular hearth. As for the place of recitation: if it is inside a room, one should go outside and dig the hearth so that it faces the honored image.
One should fashion it according to the specific rite and in accordance with the ritual rules. [The wood for] the milky fuel—
Place the aforementioned items, as well as incense and flowers, on the right side. Place the *homa* vessels on the left side.

Sitting upon a seat of *kuśa* grass, collect the mind in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). First, recite the mantra of the principal deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) once, and request that they be seated in their proper place.
Make offerings according to the ritual. We pray that the Honored One will graciously accept this *homa* food.
As for the *homa* wood, there are twelve kinds, which do not exist in this land; one may use red sandalwood or substitute it with solid milky wood.
Select branches that are straight at their tips, measuring two finger-widths—or as some say, ten finger-widths—in length; these must be freshly cut and moist. Observe them...
Place it with one side facing upward. Wash it thoroughly with scented water. Position the fine end outward and the coarse end toward the body.
Anoint both ends with milk, curd, ghee, and honey, then cast it into the hearth. As during the time of recitation, place both hands between the knees;
it should be done likewise during the homa. When the homa is completed, use pure water with the root mantra.
With the hand, move far around and sprinkle [the offerings] into the hearth. Do this three times. When the homa is entirely finished, dismiss [the deities] according to the ritual rules.
If performing the rite with ghee, honey, and oil, one should use a ladle; upon reaching the word *svāhā*, before the remaining sound has faded, pour it into the hearth.
At the beginning, perform one round of homa with a full ladle of ghee; for the middle rounds, use a small ladle.
When the homa is completed, once again offer a ladle full of clarified butter for one round of homa. Re-present the arghya water and continue with the offerings as before.
Repeat the protective mudrās and so forth, up until the dissolution of the boundary (sīmābandha), and only then may you dismiss [the deities] as explained below.
Furthermore, there is another method. If one wishes to cause others to feel respect, affection, and joy, one should invoke the person's name within the mantra;
they will immediately become joyful, compliant, and submissive.
*Hara* (translated as "to invoke") means to call out the name of the person before one. Recite it once for each invocation, completing one hundred and eight repetitions.
Even if one merely pays reverent homage, there is another method: if one lacks clothing, by reciting the mantra one will immediately obtain clothing.
Furthermore, whatever one seeks in one's mind, through recitation it shall all be attained according to one's wishes.
The Cundī Dhāraṇī is the heart-treasure of all Buddhas, like the king of maṇi jewels; because it accords with the thoughts of sentient beings, it is said that "all obtain their wishes.
Furthermore, according to the ritual method: if a person suffers pain in the body or its limbs and joints, they should empower their hands twenty-one times and rub them over the painful areas.
It will be healed immediately.
Whether for oneself or for another, it is effective in both cases.
Furthermore, there is another method: if one suffers from malaria or a headache, one may also obtain relief by touching the afflicted area with a hand empowered twenty-one times through recitation.

[The ailments] were eliminated and cured. These cases all refer to practitioners who have already perfected their prior training, or those who have long maintained the recitation of the Cundī-dhāraṇī;

therefore, they obtain immediate efficacy and verification in every instance. As for a practitioner who has only recently begun recitation, their Sanskrit pronunciation is not yet pure and their mind is not [yet focused].
If one is single-minded yet instead slanders [the rite] as being without efficacy, the transgression incurred will be even more profound.
Furthermore, there is another method: smear a small altar and take a copper bowl, filling it with pure ashes.
Have a youth press both hands upon the bowl of ashes while the reciter chants the mantra. The attendant spirit of the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) will enter the youth’s body; as for the bowl—
He immediately turned and spoke the following words. The youth then personally bound the samaya-mudrās of the three families and recited the mantras of the three families.

He then took a piece of smooth stone and passed it to the youth. The youth immediately inscribed upon the ground matters of the past and future, including auspicious and inauspicious events, good and evil omens, as well as lost or forgotten sūtras and śāstras, difficult points of meaning, mantras, and mudrās; all of these were thereby known.

[Answer: It is explained that "pervasive" (*vyāpin*) is not mentioned here; it should be understood as "one hundred and eight pervasive [recitations]. Alternatively, it is limited to holding [the substance] until the youth himself performs the mudrā and recites the mantra.
Furthermore, there is another method: when two armies are opposed to one another, write this dhāraṇī upon birch bark and suspend it from a bamboo pole.
Have a person hold it in their hand and recite the mantra; the opposing enemy will then be defeated.
The above several items are missing from other translations.
Furthermore, there is another method: if a woman has no son or daughter, one should write this mantra upon birch bark with ox-gall (gorocanā) and have her wear it;
before long, she shall have a son or daughter.
The translation by Zhi states: "Write this dhāraṇī upon birch bark and paint a youth;
wrap it in purple silk and recite it one hundred and eighty times. Place it within the hair-knot and one will conceive. Alternatively, it is said:
"The original intent of the Buddhas was to cause people to sever all afflictions such as greed and hatred; why then does this now cause people to give rise to greed?"
[Question: "Do they seek worldly affairs, fame, profit, and the like? [Answer:

"This is the inconceivable power of all Buddhas, the wondrous application of skillful means for delivering sentient beings. If there are sentient beings who are unwilling to directly seek unsurpassed bodhi,"
Furthermore, according to their desires, let them be empowered to seek [their goals] through the recitation of mantras; they shall all achieve their hearts' content.

Through the permeation of the inconceivable power of these divine mantras, their karmic offenses are extinguished and the seeds of Bodhi are established. Thus, they naturally transcend the mundane and enter the state of sagehood.
Such mantras are the realm of all Buddhas; even Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages cannot fathom their measure, let alone ordinary persons.
How could it be subject to conceptual thought? For one who possesses the eye of wisdom, though they must seek throughout the entire day, there is neither the act of seeking nor the object sought;
this is precisely what constitutes correspondence with *prajñā*. Therefore, it is not that the Buddha permits sentient beings to give rise to afflictions such as greed and the like.
Furthermore, there is another method. Should there be a woman whose husband does not treat her with respect, she should take a new flask and fill it with water.

Within the flask, she should place the seven precious gems, various efficacious medicines, the five grains, and white mustard seeds. She should tie a silk cloth around the neck of the flask and empower it by reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times.
She should then have the woman form the root mudrā and place the flask upon her head, using the water [to sprinkle her].
Upon receiving the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one immediately gains favor, love, and respect; not only does one gain respect, but one also obtains offspring who remain secure in the womb.
According to the translation by Ji, one should take a pure vessel, fill it with scented water, place it in a separate clean location, and smear it with cow dung.
At the altar, recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times. Perform this rite for all seven vases in this manner. At a pure location, establish a *maṇḍala* with incense and flowers.
Taking the perfumed water from within the vases, perform an ablution; the husband will then come to love her, and she shall also conceive.
If the wife does not love her husband, perform the aforementioned rite as well. This is according to the *dhāraṇī-sūtra* found within the Great Canon (*Tripiṭaka*).

Mantras are collectively categorized into five families: first, the Buddha Family, which refers to the mantras of all Buddhas; second, the Lotus Family, which refers to the mantras of Avalokiteśvara and other lotus-holding Bodhisattvas;
third, the Vajra Family, which refers to the mantras of Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and the various Vajra deities;
fourth, the Jewel Family, which refers to the mantras of the various devas; and fifth, the Karma Family, which refers to the mantras of all... [the text continues].
Regarding the mantras of spirits and deities, these five sections each contain five sub-sections, totaling twenty-five sections.
This present Cundī Dhāraṇī encompasses and subsumes all twenty-five sections; therefore, whatever purpose one employs it for, there is nothing that will not be accomplished.

Furthermore, there is another method: whenever the practitioner recites the mantra, they should bind the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) and recite it until the mudrā has been performed six million times upon a stūpa.

Then, whatever is sought shall be fulfilled. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, and Tārā Bodhisattva will manifest their forms before them, granting all that is desired. One may even become a king within the palace of the asuras, or...
One attains the Bodhisattva stages, or obtains long-life elixirs, or achieves the rite of *kṛtyā* (loving-kindness/attraction).

According to the translation by Jñāna, on the shore of the great ocean, or among the islands of a river, or upon a sandy beach, one uses a stūpa-shaped seal to impress the form of a stūpa into the sand.
Reciting the mantra once, one seal completes one stūpa; thus it continues.
When the count reaches six hundred thousand recitations, one will immediately behold the noble Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and others.
All their heart's desires will be fulfilled according to their wishes. Some may see him bestowing the wondrous elixirs of the immortals;

some may see him bestowing the prophecy of future Buddhahood upon them as Bodhisattvas; or he may appear before them to inquire after them, and whatever they pray for, they shall all attain the rank of a Bodhisattva. If...
If one desires to attain intelligence, take half a *liang* each of *śilācampa* (stone calamus) and ox-gall (*gorocanā*). Grind them into a powder and mix it with clarified butter (*sarpis*).
Construct a mandala before a Buddha statue and recite the mantra five thousand times; upon consuming it, one will immediately attain intelligence.
The *Vidyādharapiṭaka-sūtra* states: "If there is a practitioner who wishes to achieve the most supreme and excellent accomplishment, they must focus their mind with single-minded concentration."

Practice with diligent effort. First, by reciting the root mantra of Cundī at the edge of a great ocean shore until six hundred thousand sand stupas have been fashioned, one will certainly attain accomplishment in whatever is sought. Vajrapāṇi is also named Vajragarbha.
Furthermore, there is another method: at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) or before a great stūpa, one should recite this dhāraṇī. One will then behold the noble Saṃgha and converse with them;
siddhi will be accomplished, and one will be able to practice together with them. Thus, one immediately becomes equal to that noble Saṃgha.
The Bodhimaṇḍa is located in the kingdom of Magadha in Central India; it is so named because the Buddha sat therein and attained *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
A *caitya* is a Buddhist stūpa. This stūpa is situated within the Bodhimaṇḍa.
According to the translation by Jñāna, if one circumambulates the image of the Bodhi tree and performs recitation one million times, one will immediately behold the Buddha’s bodhi.
The Arhat will preach the Dharma for them. If they wish to follow the Bodhisattva, they shall immediately be able to follow him.

Whatever they seek shall be fulfilled according to their wishes, until they manifest in this very body as great mantra-adepts (vidyādhara), whereupon they shall be able to travel to the pure lands of the ten directions, serve all Buddhas, and hear the True Dharma.
Furthermore, if they wish to see all ghosts and spirits, they should take ox-gallstone (gorocana) and recite [the mantra] over it.
Smoke emerges; immediately apply it to the eyes and also ingest it, and one will see. The *Vidyādhara-piṭaka-vidhi* states:
"When the recitation reaches one koṭi, one attains the appearance and speech of an Arhat in person, gaining great benefit.
Thereafter, one travels together with Arhats and likewise shares their majestic power."

Furthermore, there is another method: if one recites [the mantra] one *koṭi* times atop a high mountain peak, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva will lead this person, along with five hundred and sixty others, into the palace of the Asuras.
There they shall have a lifespan of one *kalpa*, behold Maitreya Bodhisattva, and hear the True Dharma.
Having heard the Dharma, they shall attain the stages of a bodhisattva and reach the state of non-retrogression.
Regarding the term "one kalpa," this refers here to a *kṣudrakalpa* (minor kalpa), which is calculated to be one million six hundred and eighty thousand years.
[The Bodhisattva] enters the palace of the asuras to await the descent of Maitreya. The *Śūramgamasamādhi-sūtra* states: "Maitreya Bodhisattva..."
After fifty-six billion years, he was then born below in the palace of Asura. There are many such places;
for instance, as for the one entered by the Master Bhāviveka, that palace was located within a mountain crag and rocky cliff not far south of the city of Andhra in South India.
The Master used incantations to strike the rocky wall with mustard seeds, whereupon it suddenly burst open.
Open [the door]. Enter within and wait to see Maitreya Bodhisattva’s descent to be born.
Furthermore, there is another method: ascend Mount Vipula.
This mountain is located in the kingdom of Magadha; it is also said that any high mountain will suffice.
One should perform recitation before a reliquary stūpa or an image, making offerings of incense and flowers according to one's ability, and sustaining one’s life by begging for food.
From the first day of the month until the fifteenth, one should recite the dhāraṇī three hundred thousand times.
On the day the count is complete, one should fast for a full day and night and increase one's offerings twofold. By the time of the final watch of the night, one will immediately see Vajrapāṇi.
The Bodhisattva will lead the practitioner to his own palace; for the practitioner, he will then show the entrance to the asura cave.
Upon entering the cave, one obtains the celestial nectar (amṛta) and attains a lifespan equal to that of the sun and moon.
Vajrapāṇi (The Vajra-in-Hand) holds a vajra in his hand, symbolizing that internally he possesses great bodhicitta and externally he subdues all the māras of affliction.
Furthermore, his own body is firm and solid, having perfected vajra-wisdom; with the vajra, he shatters the mountain of false views and realizes vajra-samādhi.
Because he constantly holds [the vajra] in the palm of his hand, he is named Vajrapāṇi. Regarding "Bodhisattva," it is fully called *bodhisattva*.
Regarding *bodhisattva*: "Bodhi" has the meaning of "awakening," and "sattva" has the meaning of "sentient being.

This refers to one who is capable of awakening oneself and, while remaining within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), awakens all sentient beings. The Chinese translation by Jñānagupta does not mention "ascending the mountain."
It merely states "in front of a stūpa," or "in front of a Buddha image," or "in front of a śarīra-stūpa.
Regarding the initial mention of "in front of a stūpa," it may refer to one of the Tathāgata’s eight great miraculous stūpas or a stūpa for the Dharmakāya-gāthā, rather than a śarīra-stūpa.

Furthermore, there is another method: at the jeweled stupa where [the Buddha] descended from heaven via the triple-jeweled staircase, the practitioner should wander while begging for alms and recite [the mantra] ten million times (*koṭi*).
Thereupon, one will see the Bodhisattva Aparājita grant a boon, preach the sublime Dharma, and reveal the path to unsurpassed enlightenment.
Alternatively, one may see the goddess Ālidī, who leads the person into her own palace and bestows upon them the elixir of longevity. Then, one returns.
He will have a youthful appearance, be upright and pleasing, and discover hidden treasures. He will be approved by great beings and shall extensively benefit the Triple Gem.
He will receive the consolation of all Bodhisattvas, who will show him the right path until he reaches the seat of enlightenment.
If one recites this dhāraṇī, until they sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), all bodhisattvas will act as their supreme friends;

therefore, they constantly offer consolation and show them the path to enlightenment consisting of the thirty-seven factors of awakening (saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma), causing them to advance in practice until they sit beneath the Bodhi tree and attain perfect, complete enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi). Thus it is called "sitting at the site of enlightenment. Āli.

The *Dīmū* (Mother of the Bottom) is none other than Hārītī; her original name was Māṇibhadramātā (Mother of Joy). Regarding "hidden treasures": it refers to obtaining treasures from within the earth.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas permitted her to take these in order to extensively benefit all sentient beings and to make offerings to the Triple Gem;

she must not be stingy or selfish in using them for herself. The "Threefold Jewel Staircase" is located in the kingdom of Saṃkāśya in Central India. Long ago, when the Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven...
[The Buddha] went to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother. When the three months had concluded, he descended from heaven. The Lord of Devas manifested three jeweled staircases:
the central one of gold, the left of lapis lazuli, and the right of agate. The Buddha descended by the central staircase.
Later, King Aśoka erected a jeweled stūpa at that site. The Zhi translation states: "If [one performs this] before the Dharmacakra-pravartana Stūpa..."
Whether before a stūpa at the Buddha’s birthplace, before a stūpa with jeweled stairs, or before a śarīra stūpa, one should perform recitation and circumambulation for seven full weeks;
then one will behold those two bodhisattvas, and all one's wishes will be completely fulfilled.
And so forth. The *Vidyādhara-piṭaka* states: "The Bodhisattvas bestow upon the practitioner sacred medicine, which transforms his body so that it possesses extraordinary marks;
furthermore, he receives the guidance of all Bodhisattvas to realize the Path, until he swiftly sits at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)."

Furthermore, there is another method: even for one who lacks past roots of goodness, lacks the seed of bodhi, and has not cultivated the practices of bodhi, the sprout of the dharma of bodhi will arise by merely reciting it once;
how much more so for one who is able to constantly recite, remember, and uphold it?
The translation by Zhi states: "If one reads it even once, the sprouts of the faculties for the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) will immediately arise;

how much more so if one recites and maintains it without ever becoming indolent or abandoning it? By virtue of these roots of goodness, one will swiftly attain the seed of Buddhahood, and immeasurable merits will all be fully accomplished.
The translation by He Luo states: "If one obtains the opportunity to hear this Great Cundī Dhāraṇī method, [one will] swiftly..."

They shall realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. If anyone should remember, uphold, recite, and chant this Great Cundī Dhāraṇī—the Heart of the Mother of Buddhas—without ever becoming lax or abandoning it, they shall achieve the accomplishment of immeasurable roots of goodness.
When the Buddha spoke this Dharma of the Great Cundī Dhāraṇī, immeasurable sentient beings were freed from [suffering].

Having purified their defilements and attained the merit of the Great Cundī Dhāraṇī Mahāvidyā-mantra, they beheld the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the assembly of all holy ones of the ten directions; having paid homage, they departed.
The Ritual Manual for the Recitation of the Seven-Crore Cundī Dhāraṇī, translated by Jñāna, states:
According to the Sanskrit manuscript of the sūtra, there are one hundred thousand verses. I shall now briefly explain the sequence of recitation, meditative practice, and offerings.
If there are disciples of the fourfold assembly who have resolved their minds toward Bodhicitta and practice the conduct of a Bodhisattva seeking...
Those who seek swift liberation from birth and death must first enter the maṇḍala of the samaya initiation and uphold the prohibitive precepts with firm resolve, never regressing.
They should cherish the bodhisattva precepts and practices of the Mahāyāna, cultivate the four immeasurables during the four modes of conduct, and give rise to the four great vows.
They should seek to escape the three miserable realms and ensure that their minds remain undistracted in all activities.
Only then may one enter this secret dharma-gate.
If there are those who practice this dhāraṇī seeking accomplishment, they must first bathe and wear clean garments.
The Susiddhikara Sūtra states: "One should bathe at the three times of day and be provided with the three robes. Furthermore, the inner robe should be washed three times a day;
once it is dry, it should be perfumed and purified by sprinkling. One should set aside separate garments for sleeping and for bathing."
These three occasions require changing [the robes]. The undergarment (*antarvāsaka*) shall be washed once every day; when dry, it may be fumigated or sprinkled with water.
For bathing, cleansing, and for both great and small excretions, one must always use mantras to purify them by mixing them with water.
If one does not purify oneself according to the Dharma, there will be no spiritual efficacy. Thus, in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, the Buddha said: "If a bhikṣu..."
Nuns, upāsakas, and upāsikās who take me as their teacher must all wash themselves clean.

If they do not wash themselves clean, they should not circumambulate the stūpas, walk the paths of practice, pay homage to the Buddha, or recite the sūtras; the devas will not be pleased, and the dhāraṇī-mantras they uphold will have no efficacy.
Furthermore, if they perform offerings of vegetarian feasts, transcribe scriptures, or create images, the merit they obtain will be meager and thin. Thus it is said.

It is said: Regarding the method of purification (*śauca*), it is fully set forth in the Vinaya; the *Susiddhi Tantra* is identical in its prescriptions for purification, differing only in the use of mantras and mudrās, as well as in the ritual sprinkling of the body.
For bathing, purification, the removal of impurities, and the washing of hands, there are respective *dhāraṇīs*, all of which should be understood as they appear in other sources.
The *Vidyādharapiṭaka-vidhi* states: "Furthermore, recite the Amṛtakuṇḍalī..."
