Use a wiping cloth to dry [the hands], washing them until they are completely clean. Then wash both hands;
having thus attained purity, return to the maṇḍala and draw near to the noble ones. Furthermore, whenever one forms mudrās, one should use unguent to smear upon both hands.

Adorn the maṇḍala and install the principal deity according to what one’s means permit. Regarding the ritual for the maṇḍala: one should select an excellent site and construct a square altar measuring four cubits on each side, excavating it to a depth of three cubits.
This refers to the adornment of the *maṇḍala*. One should provide banners, parasols, incense, flowers, food, drink, and so forth, according to one's capacity.

Regarding the excellent site, it is as explained below: Zhi translates this as "east, west, south, and north," meaning one should measure out four *cubit* (*hasta*) on each side to construct a square altar, digging it to a depth of one *cubit*.
Remove debris, poor soil, hair, body hair, bones, ash, charcoal, insects, ants, and the like. Fill the site with excellent, pure earth and level it.
If no poor soil is found when digging, take the existing earth to fill it; if there is a surplus of earth, know that this ground is most auspicious and will swiftly bring accomplishment.
Take *gomaya* (cow dung) that has not yet fallen to the ground and purify it by mixing it with scented water.
Prepare good earth as mud. Recite the mantra of the Bodhisattva Aparājita twenty-one times to empower it, and then smear the altar.
Once the altar has been smeared, take the five purities and mix them together.

The five pure substances are cow dung, cow urine, curd, milk, and ghee. Other schools prescribe that one take the five pure substances of a yellow cow and empower them one hundred and eight times with the mantra of the Bodhisattva Aparājita, then smear them all over the maṇḍala in a clockwise direction.
In Sanskrit, it is called *maṇḍala*; in the language of China, it is called a *tán* (altar). "Altar" (*tán*) means "to give birth," because it gives rise to inexhaustible merit.
Furthermore, "altar" means "to assemble," as it is the place where boundless sages and worthies gather. Such is the method of the altar.
This is the inconceivable divine power of all Buddhas; do not give rise to doubt or hesitation. Bind it according to the ritual method, and that which you seek will surely be obtained as desired.
Whether established upon mountains or rocks, or situated within a multi-storied pavilion, or dwelling upon a boat, all worthy sages shall attain [success].
Regarding the site for the path: simply smear it with the five kinds of pure substances.
Zhi’s translation states: "If one is in the mountains or in a fine, clean house, there is no need to dig the ground; one should rely on the previous method of smearing."
Then, spread a canopy above and suspend banners on all four sides. If there is an image of the Mother of the Buddhas (*Buddhamātṛ*), place it within the maṇḍala facing west.
If there is no primary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), there should be images of various Buddhas, relics, and Mahāyāna sūtras.
One may also perform the offering while facing east.
Forming the *Ajita-mudrā*, press it upon the ground and recite the mantra seven times to consecrate the center of the maṇḍala.
Furthermore, take small portions of various medicinal herbs, the seven precious gems, and the five grains; then, dig at the center of the maṇḍala to a depth of one cubit (*hasta*).
Place the various medicines and the seven precious gems therein. Then, take the original soil to fill it completely and level it.
Press down with the right hand and recite the verses to the Earth Goddess three times to awaken the terrestrial deities. The verses are as follows:
O Devaputra, protector, who has practiced supreme conduct under the Buddhas, the Guides, and purified the stages and the pāramitās—
just as you have shattered the hosts of Māra’s army, so too shall I, the Lion of the Śākyas and Savior of the World,
subdue Māra; I shall draw the maṇḍala.
The mantra for reciting the Earth Deity is as follows: *Namo samantabuddhānāṃ vṛthivīye svāhā*.
The "Earth-Dwellers" (bhūmideva) refer to yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, nāgas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, bhūtas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, and so forth.
Mantras are also called "Sublime Words" (suvacana), meaning they flow forth from the hearts of all Buddhas; they are words that are truly subtle, wondrous, and secret.
All the devas, māras, and brahmās, as well as bodhisattvas at the stage of cause, cannot conceive of it through thought.
Having recited the verses for empowerment, one then applies sandalwood paste to the nine sacred positions so that they resemble the full moon.
The translation by Zhi states: "Grind white sandalwood and smear it to form eight mandalas, resembling the full moon or eight-petaled lotuses.
The original translation instructs that one should smear [the ground] for the nine holy positions; this refers to making offerings to the nine-syllable root mantra.
According to the translation by Jñānagupta, one should smear eight altars and prepare offerings for each of the eight lines of the complete mantra;

this may be done according to one's preference, and all methods are acceptable. Using new and pure offering vessels—such as those made of gold, silver, refined copper, conch shell, mother-of-pearl, jade, stone, porcelain, or wood—and filling them with various foods and drinks, as well as fine incense, flowers, lamps, candles, and *argha* perfumed water, one should arrange these offerings according to one’s means.

As for the *śaṅkha*, it refers to a conch-shell cup. According to the Susiddhi Tantra, one should smear the ground at the three times of the day, offer flowers, fragrant water, and various other offerings;
remove withered flowers and continuously place fresh ones; and regarding the bowls and vessels used for offerings, wash and scrub them at the three times of the day.

If a bodhisattva, whether lay or ordained, seeks accomplishment, they should first pay homage to the Buddha, perform confession, rejoice in merit, make requests, and form aspirations whenever entering the maṇḍala.
Having done so, they should take the vow to receive the bodhicitta precepts.

Based on this, when bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, or laypeople who have already received the three refuges, the five precepts, or the eight precepts enter the maṇḍala, they must all personally vow to receive the bodhicitta precepts. The Susiddhi Sūtra states:
Bathe and change clothes three times each day. At these three times, perform offerings, prostrations, repentance, sympathetic joy, requests for teaching, and the making of vows.
Recite scriptures at these three times, as well as construct maṇḍalas. Take refuge and receive the precepts at these three times, and protect yourself at these three times.
By performing the ritual in this manner, one will certainly attain accomplishment. The Zhi translation also requires that one receive the precepts at these three times.
The text includes the practices of prostrating to the Buddhas, repentance, and sympathetic joy, but lacks the sections on requesting [the Buddhas to teach] and making vows.
I have now appended the five dharmas—prostrating to the Buddhas, repentance, sympathetic joy, requesting [the Buddhas to teach], and making vows—in detail as follows.
The mantra is: Oṃ maitrīcittam utpādayāmi maitrī. *Bodhi* may also be used for *maitrī*.
*Citta* may also be used for *citta*, *jñā* for *citta*, and *pa* or *ma* for *maitrī*. It may also be [rendered as] *maitrī*.
As for "Maitreya," the *Yogācārabhūmi-vyākhyā* states: *Maitrī-citta*. This is translated as "Awakened Mind" (*bodhicitta*). The syllable *mai* serves as the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
The syllable *mai* signifies the meaning that all phenomena are without bondage.

If one can realize that the *bodhicitta* within one's own body is spontaneously accomplished (*svabhāva-siddha*), equal throughout the three periods of time, like space, and free from all characteristics, then...
To realize that the minds of all sentient beings and the minds of all Buddhas are identical to one's own mind—fundamentally pure—is to give rise to great compassion and profound pity.

Through various skillful means, one causes all sentient beings to leave suffering behind and attain liberation, reaching the ultimate state where there is neither bondage nor release; this is the vast bodhicitta.
The bodhicitta is free from all grasping at a self; it is far removed from the aggregates, sense bases, and elements, and is devoid of subject and object.
It is equal toward all phenomena, for one’s own mind is fundamentally unarisen, being empty by its very nature.
Just as all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past generated the bodhicitta, so shall I do likewise. This is called the vow to receive the bodhicitta precepts through recitation. By reciting:
By contemplating the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) even once, one attains immeasurable and boundless unconditioned merit (*asaṃskṛtakuśala*), which adorns the three modes of action (*trikarma*).

Until reaching the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), this merit remains uninterrupted; all karmic obstacles are swiftly extinguished, mantras are quickly brought to accomplishment, and the deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) appears before one.
This is as described in the "Entry into the Dharma Realm" (*Lokadhātupraveśa-parivarta*) chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where the Bodhisattva Maitreya...
The youth Sudhana speaks of the merit of the bodhicitta.
"Aggregates" (skandha) refers to the five aggregates; "bases" (āyatana) refers to the twelve bases; and "elements" (dhātu) refers to the eighteen elements, as explained elsewhere.
The ritual for receiving the bodhicitta precepts states: "The awakening mind now generated is free from all intrinsic natures and characteristics, [including] the aggregates, elements, and..."
The grasping at bases and so forth as subject and object—may all phenomena be selfless, equal like space, and fundamentally unborn within one's own mind due to the emptiness of perfect peace.
Just as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have generated the great bodhicitta, I now generate it in this same way.
The remainder is as clarified in the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter.
Having taken the vow to receive the Bodhicitta precepts, sit at ease—either fully or partially covered—with the body upright and eyes closed.
Immediately form the mudrā of meditative concentration (*samādhi-mudrā*) and visualize the Buddha-Mother Cundī in the sky, surrounded by seven koṭis of Buddhas, filling all of space.
Within this state of concentration, prostrate to all the Buddhas and the Buddha-Mother Cundī. Then, apply incense to your hands.
One should form the mudrās of commitment.
First, form the mudrā of concentration; next, form the mudrā of bowing to the Buddha; both are as described below. The Zhi translation states:
"Settle the mind in meditative sitting, eliminate all discursive thoughts, and contemplate the sentient beings of the six realms within the ocean of birth and death since time immemorial."
May those wandering through the six realms of saṃsāra all resolve to attain bodhicitta, practice the conduct of a bodhisattva, and swiftly achieve liberation.
Then, rub the hands with scented ointment and form the hand-mudrās. While forming the mudrās, cover the hands with a cloth so that others do not see them.
First, form the samaya seals of the three families, and subsequently form the other seals.
○ The Samaya-mudrā of the Buddha Family (i.e., the Samādhi-mudrā).
The Susiddhikara Sūtra states: First, within the inner chamber, one should place an image of the Honored One, or a caitya, or simply set out a seat.
Upon entering, face the Honored One, join the palms, bow the body, recite the mantra aloud, and upon entering, perform prostration.
Thereafter, one should make offerings. The mantra is: Oṃ jvalita rocani phaṭ.
Recite this seven times. Next, one should perform the samaya-mudrās and mantras of the three families.
With both hands joined in an empty-clasp (*śūnyapāṇi*), extend the two index fingers and bend them so that they rest against the side of the first joint beneath the nails of the middle fingers.
Place the two thumbs each against the base of the two index fingers; this constitutes the mudrā. Holding it at the heart, recite the mantra seven times.
Visualize the Tathāgata’s thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, appearing with such clarity as if they were right before one's eyes.

According to the translation by Ji, the hands of merit and wisdom are both turned upward; the fingers of generosity (*dāna*), precept (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) are slightly bent and pressed together.

The fingers of vigor (*vīrya*), power (*bala*), and patience (*kṣānti*) rest upon the upper joints, while the fingers of meditation (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) lean against the side of the finger of vigor. This constitutes the mudrā of the Susiddhikara Sūtra.
Translated by Tongzhi. Generosity, Precepts, Patience, Diligence, Meditation—beginning from the little finger of the right hand; Wisdom, Skillful Means, Vow, Power, and Knowledge.
Beginning from the left little finger, these are the ten pāramitās. The mantra is: Oṃ tathāgatodbhava svāhā.
*Dǔ* may be written as *dù*; *nà* may be written as *nà*. In the translation by Jñānagupta, it is rendered as *Oṃ tathāgatābhyaḥ svāhā*.
One should seal the crown of the head with the mudrā and scatter [the mantra]. The character *bó* (皤) is pronounced with a departing tone (*qùshēng*); the same applies to all subsequent instances.
By binding this mudrā and reciting the mantra, one immediately awakens all Tathāgatas, who shall all protect, mindfully regard, and empower the practitioner.
Through the touch of their radiance, all karmic obstacles and hindrances are completely extinguished, and one’s lifespan becomes long and enduring.

May merit and wisdom increase. May the noble assembly of the Buddha family provide protection and rejoice. In birth after birth, may one be free from all evil realms and be born through transformation within a lotus flower, swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

The *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra* states: "If one recites mantras upon a mountain peak, all sentient beings within the range of vision—including those who have committed the five heinous crimes or the ten evil deeds—shall all extinguish their transgressions and, in future lives, be born through transformation from lotus flowers in the pure lands of the Buddhas.
How much more so for the practitioner who upholds the mantra; shall they not be born by transformation from a lotus flower and extinguish all their sins?"
Yes. ○ For the Samaya-mudrā of the Padma-kula:
join the two hands with palms hollowed and bring them together; then extend the two index fingers, the two middle fingers, and the two ring fingers, while bending [the thumbs].

Forming the shape of a lotus, place the mudrā at the heart and recite the mantra seven times. Visualize that Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva is fully endowed with all the marks and signs of excellence, and scatter [the flowers] over the right side of the crown.
The two little fingers and the two thumbs touch one another, while the remaining six fingers are spread apart and slightly bent, like an opening lotus flower.
The marks and signs of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara are as described in the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*.
The mantra is: Oṃ (1) ba-na-muḥ (2) nā-bha-va-ya-svā-hā (3). "Ba-na" may also be written as "pat-na.
In the Zhi translation, it is rendered as: Oṃ padma-vajrāya svāhā.
By binding this mudrā and reciting the mantra, one awakens Avalokiteśvara and all the Bodhisattvas who hold lotuses.
Their radiant light touches [the practitioner], whereby all karmic obstructions are completely extinguished,
and all Bodhisattvas constantly act as one's virtuous friends.

The *Ritual for Making Offerings to the Tathāgata Amitāyus* states: "By forming this mudrā and reciting this mantra, one awakens Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and the holy assembly of the Lotus Family, who all come to bestow their empowerment upon the practitioner.
Thus, one attains purity of vocal karma; one’s speech becomes majestic and solemn, causing others to delight in hearing it, and one gains unimpeded eloquence for preaching the Dharma."
Sovereign. ○ For the Samaya-mudrā of the Vajra Family:
turn the left hand outward; place the back of the right palm upon the back of the left hand; [join] the thumbs and little fingers of both hands...
Interlock the fingers so that they form the shape of a vajra and place it at the heart. Visualize the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi and recite the mantra seven times.
Finally, release the mudrā over the left side of the head.
The Susiddhikara Sūtra states: "The six fingers between the two hands are slightly opened, like a three-pronged vajra.
These three seals are called the Great Seals (mahāmudrā). Even the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas cannot contravene them, let alone the various classes of māras."
It not only accords with the teachings but also extinguishes all transgressions and eliminates all calamities; whatever Dharma one seeks will surely be obtained in accordance with one's wishes.

As for the mudrā, the *Zhì* translation instructs that the left hand should cover and the right hand should face upward, with the thumbs and little fingers interlaced; thus the seal is formed, and it is identical to the original translation.
The mantra is: Oṃ vāruṇāpaya svāhā. Translated by Zhi, it reads: Oṃ vācchuḥ vapaye svāhā.
By binding this mudrā and reciting this mantra, all the assemblies of Vajra-saints will be awakened to provide empowerment and protection.
All karmic obstacles and transgressions shall be completely extinguished; no suffering whatsoever shall ever afflict the body, and one shall attain a vajra-like, adamantine body.
The Ritual Manual for Offerings states: "By forming this mudrā and reciting the mantra, one awakens the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha and the holy assembly of the Vajra family;
they all come to bestow their empowerment upon the practitioner, whereby one attains purity of mental action."
Realize the bodhicitta; samādhi will manifest before you, and you will swiftly attain liberation.
Following the *Jñāna* translation, form the samaya-mudrās of the three families, and then immediately form the fundamental body-mudrā of the Mother. Recite the mantra of the Mother seven times.

In the current version of this translation, the root mudrā is bound prior to the recitation while holding the rosary; however, if one wishes to bind it at another time, there is no hindrance provided it accords with reason.
This mudrā is as described in the subsequent section on the argha (offering water) mudrā.
Next, bind the second root mudrā (used for protecting the body).
Translated by Jñāna. This mudrā is used prior to holding the rosary and reciting mantras at the end [of the ritual].
Furthermore, there is a separate mudrā and mantra for expelling all celestial Māras and evil spirits; in the original translation, this mudrā and the heart-mantra are used for protection.
Afterward, one should again use the *Ajita-mudrā* mantra to ward off obstructing spirits.
Form the mudrā by interlacing the two hands with the palms facing outward; extend the two index fingers and the two thumbs straight upward, and it is thus completed.

Recite the Heart Mantra of the Mother (*Buddhamātṛ*) and seal the five places of the body: namely, the forehead, then the right shoulder, then the left shoulder, then the heart, then the throat, and finally the crown of the head.
[The ritual] above is concluded. The mantra is: Oṃ kāmare vimale jñāne svāhā.
When forming the seal for protecting the body, arouse a mind of great compassion and universally direct it toward the six realms and four modes of birth, making this vow for all sentient beings:
They are clad in the firm adamantine armor of the great vows and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
As for this "firm adamantine armor of the great vows," it means that the bodhisattva takes the four great vows as their adornment, remaining unimpeded by demons or malevolent spirits;
whether encountering adverse or favorable conditions, their mind never regresses.
Therefore, I pray that all sentient beings may don such firm adamantine armor, be free from all obstacles and difficulties, and swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi.
Having formed this thought, one immediately becomes armored in the adamantine mail;
no māras whatsoever will dare to create obstacles or difficulties.
Next, form the mudrā of the earth-bound stake:
interlace the two hands with the palms facing inward; extend the two thumbs, the two index fingers, and the two little fingers so that they touch one another.
Bend the left index finger into a hook shape and perform three pulls. Place the thumb on the ground; this completes one pull of the mudrā. Recite the mantra once.
The translation by Zhi states: Interlace the two middle fingers and the two ring fingers of both hands within the palms, with the right hand pressing down upon the left.
Bend the right index finger like a hook while keeping the left index finger straight and upright. Align the two thumbs and the two little fingers so that their faces touch one another.
The mantra is: Oṃ cundini jīrāya svāhā. Recite this once. [Then] with the seal of the Great Mother...
Pointing with the finger, touch the ground once in the manner of striking a stake; perform this three times and then cease.
By forming this mudrā and reciting the mantra to empower the boundary of the earth, it shall extend downward as far as the water’s edge, becoming like a vajra-throne.
Neither celestial Māras nor various obstructing spirits shall cause harm; with little exertion of effort, one will swiftly attain accomplishment.
All impure and foul substances within the earth shall become entirely purified through the power of the empowerment of this seal and mantra.
The practitioner should next visualize, at the center of the maṇḍala, a great eight-petaled lotus upon which is a lion throne.

Upon the throne is a jeweled pavilion, draped with various necklaces, silk banners, flags, and canopies. Rows of jeweled pillars stand in order, hanging exquisite celestial garments, spreading clouds of incense, and raining down a profusion of various flowers.
Various musical instruments are played, and there are jeweled vases and *argha* offerings, as well as celestial marvels.
For food and drink, use mani-jewels as lamps. If there is no maṇḍala, it is accomplished simply by visualizing it within space.
Having performed this visualization, one should recite this verse.
By the power of my merit, by the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment, and by the power of the Dharma-realm,
may there be universal offerings.
Having recited this verse, one then recites the mantra of the Bodhisattva Mahākāśyapa-garbha:
Oṃ (1) gaganasvabhāva (2) vajra hūṃ (3). The three syllables are in the departing tone (falling tone).
The syllable *ba* is in the departing tone. The syllable *ga* may also be written as *ga*, pronounced lightly.
By virtue of empowering these through the recitation of this mantra, the imagined articles of offering become truly no different from the real;
thus, all the noble assemblies are able to partake of them.
According to the *Amitāyurdhyāna-vidhi*, one should recite the Great Gaganagañja Dhāraṇī. First, one should form the mudrā:
join the two hands in *añjali*; interlace the two middle fingers with the right over the left, pressing them against the backs of the hands;
and clasp the two index fingers together in the shape of a jewel. Visualize that from this mudrā flow forth immeasurable articles of offering, such as garments and drinks.

Food, palaces, pavilions, and so forth—even if the practitioner’s power of visualization is weak, through the empowering force of this seal and mantra, all offering substances become truly vast and sublime offerings. Furthermore, according to another section, there is the "Offering-Birth Seal":
place the two hands at the heart in *añjali* mudrā, with the ten fingers of the right hand pressing down upon those of the left. The tips...
Intersecting them, place them again upon the crown of the head. Recite the mantra for the offering of emanation twenty-one times;
this is the syllable Oṃ. Through the inconceivable power of the Oṃ-mantra and the mudrā, they naturally pervade the entire dharmadhātu.
One should produce inexhaustible offerings such as incense, flowers, lamps, banners, pennants, jeweled canopies, robes, bedding, pavilions,
palaces, music, and hymns of praise— various implements of worship— to offer to the infinite Three Jewels of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
If one lacks food, drink, incense, flowers, and so forth, one should simply form mudrās before the image.
Recite the mantra of the syllable *Oṃ*. Naturally, there will be immeasurable offerings that universally provide for the inexhaustible Triple Gem throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
Thus, one should know that the single syllable *Oṃ* is like a *maṇi* jewel, manifesting according to the mind’s intent, just as described in this sutra.
All that is intended shall be fully accomplished. Furthermore, this syllable *Oṃ* is the phoneme of all mantras;
it is capable of generating the meaning of all mantra syllables. For this reason, it is proclaimed at the beginning of all mantras.
Next, form the Seal of the Precious Chariot (the character for *che* is pronounced *chā* [level tone]; the character for *lù* is pronounced *lù*).

With both hands, interlace the fingers inwardly with palms facing upward. Cross the two index fingers horizontally so they touch at their tips, and press the bases of the index fingers with the two thumbs.
Visualize the seven-jeweled chariot; the messengers of the Buddha-family mount these seven-jeweled chariots and travel through the void.
Then, having departed, he went to the peak of the realm of form, the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, within the palace of Vairocana Buddha,
and recited the mantra seven times.
The translation by Zhi states: First, cross the two hands inward with the right pressing upon the left, then open the palms upward.
Extend the two index fingers straight so that their tips touch. Move the two thumbs back and forth against the tips of the two middle fingers;
this completes the mudrā. One should then visualize Vairocana Tathāgata within the celestial palace of Akaniṣṭha, together with the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages.
Surrounded by a retinue, within the assembly, one should invoke the Noble Mother Bhṛkuṭī Tārā, riding upon a chariot adorned with the seven precious jewels.
Upon it is a seat of white lotus flowers, and upon that seat is her form exactly as depicted. One should bring her to mind within the heart.
It is as if it were before one's eyes. Akaniṣṭha Heaven—here translated as the Heaven of Ultimate Form—is the highest heaven of the Realm of Form;
it is also called the Heaven of the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra).
The mantra is: Oṃ (1) dhu ru dhu ru hūṃ (2). The letter *ru* is pronounced with the retroflex tongue.
According to the translation by Jñāna, the word *hūṃ* is absent; instead, the word *svāhā* is present.
By virtue of reciting the mantra, performing mudrās, and receiving empowerment, the seven-jeweled chariot ascends to the summit of the Form Realm (Rūpadhātu).
The Buddha-Mother Cundī, together with the eight great bodhisattvas and the assembly of holy beings, surrounded by their retinues, mounts the seven-jeweled chariot.
The eight great bodhisattvas are: first, Avalokiteśvara; second, Maitreya; third, Ākāśagarbha;
fourth, Samantabhadra; fifth, Vajrapāṇi; sixth, Mañjuśrī; seventh, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin; and eighth, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.
If Vairocana Buddha internally realizes the wisdom of samādhi, sixteen bodhisattvas then flow forth.
1. Vajrasattva; 2. Vajrarāja; 3. Vajrarāga; 4. Vajrasādhu; 5. Vajraratna; 6. Vajratejas; 7. Vajraketu; 8. Vajrahāsa; 9. Vajradharma;
10. Vajratīkṣṇa; 11. Vajrahetu; 12. Vajrabhāṣa; 13. Vajra... [text truncated]
14. Vajrapāla; 15. Vajrayakṣa; 16. Bodhisattva Vajramuṣṭi. The *Yogavibhaṅga-āryabhūmi-sādhanadharma-paryāya* states:
"Mantra and dhāraṇī constitute the fundamental school [of this teaching].
They are the secret teachings of all Tathāgatas and the dharma-gate for cultivating and realizing the noble wisdom of self-awakening. It also states:
This bodhisattva fully receives the pure precepts and immeasurable modes of conduct. They enter the ocean-like assemblies of all Tathāgatas and receive the rank of a bodhisattva.
Having transcended the three realms and received the Buddha’s commands, they possess the gates of samādhi.
Through these causes and conditions, they suddenly accumulate merit and vast wisdom, such that they never regress from unsurpassed enlightenment.

Free from all devas, māras, all afflictions (*kleśa*), and all karmic obstructions, one realizes and merges with the four bodies of the Buddha in every thought-moment—namely, the *svābhāvika-kāya* (nature body), the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (enjoyment body), the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (emanation body), and the *nisyanda-kāya* (flowing-out body).
One thereby fulfills the five wisdoms and the thirty-seven unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*). Thus, the emanation body of the Tathāgata, within Jambudvīpa in Magadha...

In the country of [Śrāvastī], at the Bodhimaṇḍa, having attained *samyak-saṃbodhi*, he preached the teachings of the Three Vehicles for bodhisattvas prior to the stages, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary beings.
Whether speaking with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) or according to his own definitive intent (*svābhiprāya*), he employed various capacities and various skillful means;
through practicing in accordance with the Dharma, they obtained the fruits of human and celestial realms, or attained the three [vehicles].

Riding upon the fruit of liberation, they may advance or retreat; regarding unexcelled bodhi, only after three great incalculable eons of diligent and arduous practice do they finally attain buddhahood.

They are born in royal palaces and pass away between the twin trees, leaving behind bodily relics for which stupas are erected and offerings made, thereby experiencing the supreme and wondrous karmic fruits of humans and devas as well as the causes for nirvana—this is not the same as the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Vairocana Tathāgata [was seated] in the palace of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven of the fourth dhyāna at the summit of the form realm.
There, all Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas who have perfected the ten stages gathered like clouds, filling the entirety of space and pervading the Dharma-realm.
To prove this awakening, body and mind suddenly realize unsurpassed bodhi.
As the Buddha of Self-Enjoyment, he emanates immeasurable bodhisattvas from his own mind, all of whom share the same nature—that is, the vajra-nature.
They receive the position of consecration from the Tathāgata Vairocana. Those bodhisattvas each proclaim the gateways of the three secrets as an offering to Vairocana.
Vairocana Buddha and all the Tathāgatas then requested empowerment and instruction. Vairocana Buddha said:

"In the future, you shall become those of the Supreme Vehicle in immeasurable worlds, enabling them to attain the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of both the mundane and supramundane realms in this very life.
If one explains according to the sequence, there will be discrepancies between the preceding and the following; this is based on [the nature of] karmic retribution."
The Buddha of the Body (*kāya-buddha*) suddenly realizes the three types of pure karma of body, speech, and mind, which pervade the entire *dharmadhātu*. Within each and every *dharmamukha*,
each and every principle (*naya*), and each and every pore, limb, and mark of excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space,
they exist without mutual obstruction, each abiding in its original position, thereby constituting the self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga*) of the all-illuminating Vairocana.

The Body [of Transformation] and the Body of Enjoyment for Others. If explained according to the sequence of the two vehicles, it is impossible to realize the fruit of the Path without fully cultivating the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

To realize the Buddha of Self-Enjoyment Body, one must necessarily attain the wisdom of the thirty-seven *samādhis* to achieve the fruit of Buddhahood. (From the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Sanskrit manuscript)

The *Gāthāsaṃgrahaparivarta* states: "The essential nature (*svabhāva*), enjoyment (*sambhoga*), transformation (*nirmāṇa*), and the concordant flow (*niṣyanda*)—these thirty-six Buddha virtues are all identical to the Essential Nature Body (*svabhāvakāya*). Together with the Dharmadhātu Body, they total thirty-seven.
By means of the empowerment of the majestic power of the wisdom that internally realizes the unsurpassed Vajradhātu within these thirty-seven, one suddenly realizes Vairocana.

From his body, immeasurable *uṣṇīṣa*-dharma-bodies stream forth from the mark of the invisible crown of the head (*anavalokitamūrdha-lakṣaṇa*). They gather like clouds in the air to form a dharma assembly.
Their radiance completely covers all, like the *cakra* of a stupa. Having fulfilled the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), they cannot be seen by anyone.
They secretly bestow grace upon sentient beings, causing all karmic obstacles of body and mind to be utterly extinguished. None are able to know this, even though it is not...
They are able to know and to extinguish all sufferings, and are reborn in the happy realms.
From the light, sixteen bodhisattvas and the great protectors of the eight directions—both internal and external—emanate in succession;
their light shines upon and touches the evil realms, forming the tiers of a stūpa that guards the stūpas of all Buddhas and the palaces of the dharma-realm, manifesting as a complete body.
This is the realization of the body of Vairocana, the Tathāgata of the Vajradhātu, who shines everywhere.
Thus one knows that the Buddha-mother Cundī flows forth from the body of Vairocana, and that the Cundī mantra is the Dharma realized within the inner minds of all Buddhas;
therefore, it is said to have been spoken by seven koṭis of Tathāgatas, for it is capable of giving birth [to all dharmas].
Because [this mudrā] belongs to all Buddhas, it is called the "Buddha-Mother.
Next, for the mudrā of the Invoking Chariot, follow the previous mudrā;
however, turn the two thumbs toward the body and push against the tips of the two middle fingers. This completes it. Recite the mantra seven times.
Pervasive. The mantra is as follows: Namaḥ siddhy-adhivikāya (1) tathāgatāya (2) oṃ vairocaniye (3) kariṣyāmi (4)
*Svāhā* (4). *Namaḥ* may also be written as *na-ma*.
*Raṅ* may also be written as *lǎng*, or as *lán*. *Nyi* may also be written as *qí*. *Gata* should be written as *nièdǔ*.
*Nyā* may also be written with the character *niáng* in the third tone (*shǎngshēng*). *Kali* may also be written as *jiāluó*.
Through the empowerment of reciting the mantra, the assembly of noble ones comes from their own lands and dwells in the air above the ritual site.
In the translation by Jñāna [Guṇabhadra], this mantra and mudrā are not present; he merely uses the subsequent mantra and mudrā to invite them.
For those who practice the path of mantras, success is achieved by following any one of these methods accordingly.
Next, perform the mudrā for inviting the Honored One (the Honored One being the Mother Guanyin, Cundī) to descend from the celestial chariot to the ritual site.
Using the same first root mudrā as before, beckon with the two thumbs toward oneself and recite the mantra three times.

The first is the Fundamental Seal (*mūla-mudrā*). This is the same as the aforementioned seal of the Buddha Family (*buddha-kula*). The subsequent statement "according to the preceding fundamental seal" refers to this.
The *Jñāna* translation states: "With the two thumbs, beckon [the deity] three times with a coming-and-going motion.
Visualize the Noble One descending from the precious chariot into the ritual arena (*maṇḍala*), onto a seat of white lotus. The *Susiddhikara Sūtra* requests: "Now there is..."
"O [Name], for the sake of [specific matter], I respectfully invite you. I humbly entreat the Venerable One to descend to this ritual site by virtue of your original vow.
I pray that you will deign to show compassion and accept this *argha* water and these humble offerings.

At the time of making this request, one should prostrate with a sincere heart and address the invitation three times. If one lacks sincerity, even though one recites many mantras, they shall all be in vain.
With earnestness, add the syllable *eḥi*. This is even more secret;
it swiftly fulfills one's wishes. The mantra is: Oṃ cale cule cuṇḍe eḥi ye hi sarvathā svāhā.
"Ha" (drawn out) is pronounced with a departing tone. Translated by Zhi as: Oṃ cili cili cundhe, ehe yehi.
*Bhagavati svāhā. Gakṣe.* (The four characters have the same pronunciation. The character *zhan* is likely a variant of *ji*.
The character *dang* should be pronounced lightly. The Susiddhi Tantra states: "Having performed the invitation, speak these words:"
"Welcome, Venerable One! Out of compassion for us, you have descended to this place of practice.
We pray that you will again look upon us with pity and sit upon this seat to accept our humble offerings. With sincere hearts, we repeatedly prostrate ourselves and address the Honored One, saying:

'Out of great compassion and pity, and by virtue of your original vow, you have deigned to descend here. This was beyond our power to arrange; it must have been through your own effort that these offerings were prepared.'"
First offer scented ointment; next, bestow flowers and so forth; again, offer incense; next, offer food and drink;
finally, light lamps, following this sequence.
Next, to bind the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Aparājita for the purpose of expelling obstructors:
with both hands, the right presses down upon the left; interlace the fingers within to form fists, and extend the two middle fingers so that their tips touch.
This completes it. Rotate it three times to the right around the body while reflecting thus: "All obstructors, Vināyakas, and all evil spirits..."
The deity fled far away. The assembly of holy beings who had come did not transgress their original samaya, but remained there out of great compassion.
May they grant their protection.
Those who cultivate the practice of mantra and mudrā, as well as practitioners of seated meditation, must first employ mantras and mudrās to eliminate all demonic obstacles.
Therefore, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "Even Bodhisattvas of the ten stages still rely on dhāraṇīs for protection; how much more so for ordinary beings? As the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* says:
"If one sits in the place of enlightenment without maintaining dhāraṇīs, it is impossible for their body and mind to remain far removed from demonic activities.
The *Siddhi-sūtra* states: "If one wishes to accomplish various other matters, one should..."
When one is about to dispatch those who possess obstacles, if they are not cleared away, there is fear that they may cause harm later;
therefore, one must first perform the rite of dispatching.
The mantra is as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānām (1) Oṃ (2) hulu hulu (3) caṇḍali (4) maṇḍe svāhā (5). [Caṇḍa may be written as Caṇḍa; ṅgi may be written as gi;
li as ri. The Vidyādhara-piṭaka states: "This mantra is capable of accomplishing [all aims]."
Regarding all matters. ○ Next, for the mudrā of the wall boundary (*prākāra-sīmā*), follow the previous earth boundary mudrā:
bend the right index finger and extend the left index finger; rotate three times to the right, as close as desired according to one's intention.
It will immediately become a city as firm and solid as a vajra. Even the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas cannot transgress it, let alone others who are difficult to subdue.
Vināyakas, venomous insects, and those with sharp fangs and claws will be unable to approach it.
The *Amitāyur-dhyāna-vidhi* states: "Visualize blazing flames flowing forth from the mudrā.
Rotate the mudrā clockwise around the body three times, according to the size of one's intention, forming a vajra-flame boundary wall in all directions to ward off all māras and evil persons."

Tigers, wolves, lions, and all venomous insects cannot approach [such a person]. The *Shenbian shu* (Commentary on Spiritual Transformations) states: "The practitioner who upholds the mantra receives the homage of all Buddhas.
Thus, the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-gāthā* says: "All Tathāgatas of the worlds in the ten directions protect and attend to those who receive and uphold [the mantra] with homage.
Since even the Buddhas offer homage to the one who upholds the mantra, how could anyone dare [to harm them]?
As for those who transgress: Vināyaka, here translated as "Pig-Headed Elephant-Trunked One. The mantra is: Oṃ jñāne prakarṣaya svāhā.
The Master Zhi translates the character *ṅa* as *ni*. Recite this three times. With the mudrā, sweep it to the right three times.

○ Next, form the Net-Boundary Mudrā for the upper direction, following the previous Wall-Boundary Mudrā. Extend the left index finger and press the right over it; cross them at the middle joints, and it is formed. Recite:
Recite this mantra three times.
According to the translation by Zhi, it corresponds to the Wall-Boundary Seal (Sīmā-bandhana-mudrā). Open [the hands] and place them facing upward:

press the tip of the right thumb against the tip of the left index finger, and press the tip of the left thumb against the tip of the right index finger; with the little fingers remaining as before, touching each other, the seal is formed.
The mantra is: Oṃ jñānīna-vajrasvāhā. The character *ja* is pronounced as *tsa-la*;
the character *ni* is translated as *ni*; the character *na* is pronounced as *lo*. Recite this three times.

Pervade [all directions]. Following the sun, perform three brandishing motions with the mudrā according to the specific section. Then, place the mudrā upon the crown of the head and rotate it to the right before releasing it.
By virtue of reciting the mantra, binding the mudrā, and performing this empowerment, there is immediately formed a vajra net that is firm, solid, and indestructible.

The *Amitāyur-dhyāna-vidhi* states: "By the power of the empowerment of the mudrās and mantras, a vajra net of solid firmness is spread above, such that even the gods of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin realm cannot create obstacles.
The practitioner’s body and mind become peaceful and blissful, and samādhi is easily attained."
Next, form the mudrā for sealing the fire enclosure:
with the left hand, cover the back of the right hand so that they overlap (leaving no gap). Straighten and erect both thumbs; this completes it.
Recite the mantra three times and circumambulate three times to the right. Visualize that outside the vajra wall, there is a great vajra flame encircling it.
The *Zhìyì* (Zhiyi) translation states: "Secretly cover the back of the right hand with the left hand so that they overlap.
Straighten both thumbs and space them about two *cùn* apart. The *Amitāyurdhyāna-vidhi* states: "Visualize immeasurable flames of light streaming forth from this mudrā.
Rotate the mudrā three times to the right; then, outside the vajra-wall, there will be a surrounding encirclement of flames."
It immediately becomes a firm and pure fire element.
The mantra is: Oṃ āsraṃ gīṇi hūṃ phaṭ (with a half-sound). (2)
The three characters are in the departing tone (去聲). The character 莽 (mǎng) is in the entering tone (上聲); it is also written as 摩 (mó), or 𦙠 (mó), or 瞢 (méng) with a level tone (引).

It is also written as 擬 (nǐ), or 儗 (nǐ). The *Susiddhikara Sūtra* instructs that it should be recited with a throaty sound (*kaṇṭha-śabda*). In the translation by Jñānagupta, it is rendered as *oṃ asama*.
"Muḥ svāhā. By binding this mudrā and reciting this mantra, one achieves a great protective seal that is tightly closed, such that no māras can enter.
Next, perform the *argha* mudrā.
*Argha* is also written as *aga* or *āga*; this is translated as "vessel. Any vessel used for making offerings is termed *argha*.
This refers to filling the *argha* vessel with water scented with saffron, camphor, white sandalwood, and so forth.

One should offer [the water] within an exquisite vessel. These vessels may be made of gold, silver, precious gems, copper, stone, clay, wood, conch shells, or even lotus leaves or the leaves of milk-exuding trees;

all such are suitable for *argha* offerings. Some say that among ritual methods, a vessel made of refined copper is the most excellent for *argha*. The Susiddhikara Sūtra states: "In performing the *śāntika* rite..."
One should use a white vessel; place a small amount of wheat and milk therein to perform the *pauṣṭika* rite.
One should use a yellow vessel; one should place sesame seeds and curd therein to perform the *ābhicāruka* rite.
One should use a black vessel; one should provide millet and cow urine, or else one's own blood. The remainder is explained below.
Interlace the two hands with the palms facing inward. Straighten the two middle fingers so that their tips touch. Use the two index fingers to pinch the backs of the two middle fingers.

The *svabhāvakāya* (self-nature body) and the *dharmadhātukāya* (dharma-realm body) together constitute thirty-seven [qualities].

These are the thirty-seven uncommon Buddha-dharmas (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), which are not shared by any other śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas. As translated by Śikṣānanda of the Tang Dynasty:
"The self-nature body, the enjoyment body, the transformation body, and the further manifested transformation; these are the thirty-six Buddha-virtues."

this means that mantras are the secret dharma of all Buddhas, transmitted only from Buddha to Buddha, and do not admit of interpretation by others; one should simply maintain their recitation without the need for forced explanation.

Second is the gate of forceful exposition. This refers to taking up any single syllable within a mantra and, whether as a person or as a phenomenon, encompassing it horizontally and vertically through sovereign liberation.
To state the essential point: within a single syllable, there are inexhaustible dharma-gates.
When all explanations are exhausted, that is precisely the meaning of the *dhāraṇī* syllables.
