One thereby attains mastery; there is nothing, whether mundane or supramundane, that one does not thoroughly comprehend. Regarding the middle three grades:
if one achieves the lower grade, one shall become a king among the mantra-siddhas, living for countless years with merit and wisdom beyond compare in the three realms.
If one achieves the middle grade, one shall attain supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and travel to other worlds.
A wheel-turning monarch lives for one kalpa. If one achieves the superior grade, one realizes the stage of a bodhisattva from the first bhūmi upward.
If one achieves the upper three grades, and if one achieves the lower grade, one attains the stage of a bodhisattva from the fifth bhūmi upward.
If one achieves the middle grade, one attains the stage of a bodhisattva from the eighth bhūmi upward. If...
The superior grade of accomplishment involves the transformation of the three secrets into the three bodies (trikāya), whereby one attains the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi within this very lifetime.
This constitutes the nine grades of accomplishment for the mantra practitioner. If one seeks directly to become a Buddha, there is no need to seek the middle or lower grades;
one should instead seek the three superior grades of accomplishment. The remainder is as explained below regarding the *puṣṭi* (increasing) rites.
Dharmaprabha, then form the seal of meditative concentration (*samādhi-mudrā*). Straighten the body and close the eyes; clarify the mind and still the thoughts.
Within the chest of the body, there shall appear a brilliant, perfect luminosity, like the full moon—pure, bright, and radiant. Arouse great diligence and resolve to attain realization. If one can...
Through diligent and focused practice, one will surely perceive the fundamentally pure mind. Within this perfect luminosity, visualize the syllable *Oṃ*;
arrange the remaining eight syllables in a clockwise rotation upon this perfect luminosity. During meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one must clearly perceive the characters of the mantra.
Once the mind is no longer distracted and concentration is attained, it corresponds with the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Thereupon, draw a circle.
Regarding the "Bright Moon Disc":
as for forming the seal of concentration (*samādhi-mudrā*), one interlaces the two hands with the backs facing outward and places them beneath the navel, palms upward;
alternatively, one may extend both hands with palms facing upward, placing the right hand over the left, with the two thumbs touching their nails. Rest [the hands] thus.
Below the navel wheel. Furthermore, the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra-vidhi* states: Interlace the two hands with the palms facing outward;
join the backs of the two index fingers and extend them straight upward from the middle joints; press the two thumbs against the two index fingers.
These three mudrās—by forming any one of them—one is able to perform this visualization of the Perfectly Luminous (*vimala-prabhāsa*). This is called...
Regarding the yoga of recitation, Guṇabhadra’s translation states: "If one seeks liberation and wishes to swiftly emerge from birth and death, one should perform this samādhi-yoga contemplation.
For those who maintain mindfulness of the unconditioned and the innumerable, they should visualize their own mind as a full moon, serene and pure, with its interior and exterior clearly distinct.
One should place the syllable Oṃ within the heart of that moon, and [place] the syllable Che-li..."
The syllables *HŪṂ*, *HRĪḤ*, *CUNDĪ*, and *SVĀHĀ* proceed from the front, circling clockwise along the rim of the wheel.
Contemplate the meaning of each individual syllable in sequence, ensuring they correspond with the mind without any error or confusion.
The *Vidyādharapiṭaka-vidhi* (Ritual Manual of the Vidyādhara Treasury) arranged by Yuánmíng states: "The syllable Oṃ is the root of Buddha Vairocana;
the syllable La is the root of the Great Wheel Vidyārāja; and the syllable Li is the root of the Great Wrathful Vidyārāja Acala."
Furthermore, the root syllable *ma* is the fundamental essence of Hayagrīva;
the syllable *li* is the fundamental essence of Amoghapāśa Bodhisattva and also of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva;
the syllable *bhaṃ* is the fundamental essence of Mahācunda Bodhisattva; and the syllable *ni* is the fundamental essence of Vajrasattva Bodhisattva.
The syllable *Sā* is the root of the Bodhisattva Ekajaṭā; the syllable *Ha* is the root of the Vidyārāja Vajranakhī.
Next, one should contemplate the meaning of the seed-syllables of the alphabet.
These nine sacred syllables can produce all other syllables; therefore, they are called "mother-letters" (*mātṛkā*).
As for the term "seed" (*bīja*), it carries the meaning of "that which draws forth and produces" and "that which gathers and sustains.

Taking the first syllable as the seed, all the contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) pertaining to the subsequent syllables is drawn forth and gathered into that initial syllable. If one attains the gateway of the syllable *Oṃ*, there is secret correspondence. Thus:
Having attained the inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas, one then awakens to the fact that all dharmas are fundamentally unarisen.

"Inexhaustible" is spoken of in terms of universal pervasion, while "unborn" is expressed in terms of the ultimate limit. Because one awakens to the fact that all dharmas are fundamentally unarisen, one immediately realizes the emptiness of all dharmas.
Since all dharmas enter into the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), they are neither arising nor ceasing; thus, one awakens to all [dharmas]...
The Dharma transcends the path of speech; therefore, it is ineffable. The characteristics of phenomena are equal, like the falling of a great rain;
hence, it is called "equality. By focusing one's attention and contemplating and observing each and every syllable, all practices and vows will be fully realized.
The syllable *Oṃ* signifies the meaning of the three bodies (*trikāya*), and it also signifies that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are fundamentally unarisen.

The translation by Jñāna states: "The gateway of the syllable *Oṃ* signifies the non-arising and non-ceasing of the flowing stream [of existence], and it is the most supreme meaning among all phenomena."
The character "Zuo" (左) signifies that all phenomena (*dharma*) are neither arising nor ceasing;
Zhi’s translation renders this as "the meaning of non-action regarding all phenomena.
The character "Li" (禮) signifies that the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena are unobtainable. The character "Zu" (祖) signifies that all phenomena are without birth or cessation.
The character *yi* (義) is translated by Zhi as "the meaning of the non-arising and non-abiding of all phenomena.
The character *li* (禮) is "the meaning of the stainlessness of all phenomena. The character *zhun* (準) is "the meaning of the peerless awakening to all phenomena. The character *ni* (泥)...
The syllable *ja* signifies that all phenomena are without grasping or abandoning. The syllable *svā* signifies that all phenomena are equal and beyond verbal expression.
The syllable *ha* signifies that all phenomena are without cause.
Regarding all phenomena, this is the meaning of causeless, quiescent, and non-abiding nirvāṇa.
Because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, one attains non-arising and non-ceasing.
Because they are non-arising and non-ceasing, one attains the non-apprehension of marks. Because there is no apprehension of marks, one attains the absence of arising and ceasing.
Because there is neither arising nor ceasing, one attains stainlessness. Because of stainlessness, one attains peerless awakening.
Because of peerless awakening, one attains non-acceptance and non-rejection. Because of non-acceptance and non-rejection, one attains equanimity beyond verbal expression.
Because of equanimity beyond verbal expression, one attains the absence of cause and effect. This is the characteristic of Prajñā.
One should enter the ultimate truth by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method; in reality, one realizes the suchness of the dharmadhātu.
Having completed the recitation within this samādhi:
This means that by realizing that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, one attains non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) through equality and non-duality.
This is in accord with the *prajñāpāramitā*, which is characterized by neither knowledge nor attainment.

By taking this wisdom of non-apprehension as a skillful means (*upāya*), one enters into the supreme ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and realizes the suchness (*tathatā*) of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This is the suchness of the dharma-realm.

The ocean cannot be explained by words; it is the realm of the Buddha, realized through the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*svasaṃvedana-jñāna*), and is not something that can be known through conceptualization or discrimination.
Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the spoken letters": although letters are established, they all have the meaning of being without letters.
Since there are no letters, one must carefully contemplate each and every aspect of the meaning, beginning again and again in a continuous cycle.
It is indeterminate and non-conceptual. It cannot be severed. That which is not severed is the supreme meaning of the continuous flow that is neither arising nor ceasing;
therefore, it is "non-action," which is the meaning of non-action. ... [as it says] ... up to:
"causeless tranquility and non-abiding nirvāṇa" is the meaning of causeless tranquility and non-abiding nirvāṇa. Therefore, it is neither arising nor ceasing.
Supremely uninterrupted and revolving in cycles, this is called the recitation of samādhi.
According to various dhāraṇī sūtras, there are many methods for the practice of upholding and reciting; here, six are briefly set forth. The first is the upholding of samādhi.
This is also called the yoga-holding (yogadhāraṇī). One simply visualizes the syllables arranged within the moon of the mind, as clarified by the method for arranging syllables in the root sūtra.
Second is the holding of inhalation and exhalation: within the very process of inhalation and exhalation, one visualizes the mantra syllables of the Brahmī script.
If the breath goes out, the syllables go out; if the breath comes in, the syllables come in. Each syllable is distinct and clear, as bright as a string of lustrous pearls, without interruption.
When the breath goes out, visualize the nine sacred Brahma-syllables within the moon disc of one’s own heart.
The syllables are linked like a chain, each emitting five-colored light that flows from one’s own mouth into the Bodhisattva Cundī.
Within the mouth, arrange [the syllables] clockwise inside the moon-disc of the Bodhisattva’s heart.
Just as when the breath enters, imagine that the syllables within the moon-disc of the Bodhisattva’s heart are linked together like a chain, each emitting five-colored light rays.
These emerge from the Bodhisattva’s mouth and flow into one’s own mouth, where they are arranged clockwise within the moon-disc of one’s own heart. Thus, having completed this, it begins again.
First, contemplate this: the three types of mantra-holding. Fourth is the holding of vocal sound, also known as the holding of subtle sound;
one should merely ensure it is heard by one's own ears, neither too slow nor too fast. The tongue does not reach the palate, but moves slightly within the mouth. The teeth are held firmly.
Recite each syllable clearly and distinctly. Fifth, recite with a loud voice so that others may hear it and thereby extinguish their transgressions;

this must be done with consideration for the timing. If there are those who lack faith nearby, hearing the sound might cause them to give rise to slander, whereby they would incur heavy karmic retribution;
in such cases, one should simply recite in a low voice. Sixth, the "subduing demons" recitation: internally take compassion as the foundation, while externally manifesting majestic wrath.
This is the mudrā. One should recite it with a frowning brow and a stern voice, as prescribed in the subsequent *ābhicāruka* rites.
Furthermore, there are two types of recitation: first, recitation without a fixed number, which means reciting constantly and without interruption without using a rosary to count;
second, recitation with signs, which means counting on a rosary and must be limited by a specific daily quota.
The number [of recitations] must not be deficient. From among the eight aforementioned types of recitation, employ whichever one is appropriate;
recite according to the ritual method without interruption, and the supreme fruit you pray for will certainly be accomplished. This is based on the version translated by Vajrabodhi.
Furthermore, various recitations have been produced; thus, the version translated by Jñānagupta next explains the visualization method for seeking vows through Cundī, stating:
"If one seeks non-discrimination, one should visualize non-discrimination and the absence of mental recollection.
If one seeks the signless and formless, one should visualize syllables and the absence of syllabic recollection. If one seeks the gate of non-duality, one should visualize..."
If one seeks the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*), one should visualize four arms. If one seeks the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), one should visualize six arms.

If one seeks the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅga-mārga*), one should visualize eight arms. If one seeks the perfection of the ten perfections (*daśa-pāramitā*) and the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), one should visualize ten arms.
If one seeks the Tathāgata’s universally pervasive and vast ground, one should visualize ten [arms].
If one has two arms, and seeks the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), one should visualize eighteen arms; this is according to the method for visualizing painted images.
If one seeks the thirty-two marks (*lakṣaṇa*), one should visualize thirty-two arms.
If one seeks the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates, one should visualize eighty-four arms. Through such visualization and contemplation as described above, one shall enter into all things.
The Tathāgata’s gate of samādhi is a ground that is profoundly deep, vast, and inconceivable. It is the station of right mindfulness;

it is right suchness and right liberation. Having performed the recitation, contemplation, and practice, if one wishes to exit the maṇḍala, one must again perform, in the previous sequence, the binding of mudrās, the offering of incense, lamps, food and drink, hand-gestures (*hasta-mudrā*), worship, and repentance. Follow [the ritual].

Rejoicing and making a vow, one immediately forms the first fundamental seal (*mūla-mudrā*) mentioned previously and recites the fundamental dhāraṇī seven times, scattering it over the crown of the head.
Then, one again forms the previous carriage seal (*ratha-mudrā*), and so forth.
One should bind the Root Mudrā. Next, bind the Bathing Mudrā. Next, bind the Five Offerings Mudrās.
Next, recite praises and present the argha water. Next, bind the Asamogha Mudrā and rotate it once counter-clockwise.
Dissolving the Boundaries (*Sīmā-bandha-vimocana*). This refers to binding the seal of the previous fire-courtyard (*agni-koṭṭa*) and reciting the *Asamāhita-mantra*.
Turning once to the left, one dissolves all the boundaries previously established. The *Vidyādharapiṭaka-vidhi-sūtra* states: "Furthermore, perform offerings, praises, and confessions."
[The practitioner] says, "I apologize. What I have offered above has been utterly lacking in excellence. I only pray that the Bodhisattva will grant me the joy of giving.

Then, having presented *argha* water, one performs prostrations. When the ritual procedure is completed, one dismisses the worthy deities (*ārya*), again performs the protection of the body (*rakṣā*), and next forms the *asamanjñi* mudrā.
Next, bind the seal of the precious chariot (*ratna-ratha-mudrā*).
Among these seals, all should be bound according to the preceding method. As for the "chariot" (*ratha*), it is the general name for a great carriage.
In this land, the Yellow Emperor first devised it; the ceremonial vehicle mounted by the Son of Heaven is called the "Jade Chariot" (*yu-lu*). The present "precious chariot" is that of the Buddha.

The vehicle upon which his mother rode was provided with a canopy and awning, from which hung various flower tassels. Bells were suspended on all four sides, and it was surrounded by railings inlaid with the seven treasures and adorned in every way.
With the thumbs pointing outward, push the tips of the middle fingers away to escort the Noble One back to his original palace.
Translated by Zhìzǔn: With both thumbs pointing outward, push the tips of the two middle fingers three times while reciting the mantra three times.
The mantra for offering is as follows:
Oṃ jvale jvalini jvāle jvālini gaccha gaccha bhagavati vaśya-vaśyānāṃ puṇyāgamānaya svāhā.
The character "che" (車) should be pronounced as "he-qie" (何切). "Gecche gecche" (蘖車蘖車) is the phrase for sending forth;
"pūrvam āmantrita-ratha-karṣaya" (前請輅車羯哩灑耶) is the phrase for inviting.
Next, bind the samaya-mudrās of the three families, reciting each mantra once.
Pay homage to the Buddha, perform repentance as before, rejoice in merit, entreat [the Buddhas] to remain, make vows, and dedicate the merit toward unsurpassed bodhi.
Then, walk about as you please, recite Mahāyāna sūtras such as the Avataṃsaka and the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, seal stūpas and images, bathe the śarīra, circumambulate to the right, and contemplate.
The six recollections. By means of this accumulation of merit, dedicate it toward the *siddhi* sought by oneself.
According to the translation by Zhi, one should recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, or the *Avataṃsaka*, or the *Anantamukha*, or the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, or the *Laṅkāvatāra*.
One should contemplate and lecture upon the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the *Mahāyāna-śāstra*, and other such texts.

Alternatively, using the seal of the seven *koṭi* Buddhas and their stūpas, one may imprint it upon fragrant clay, sand, or paper as much as one desires; if one has achieved merit through recitation, [the results will be accordingly].
Regarding the objects of focus as described in the sūtras, one should clearly understand each part in its proper sequence. The Susiddhi Tantra states:

"In order to purify the mind, one should constantly maintain the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), focusing the mind on a single object without distraction. First is the recollection of the Buddha."
Second is mindfulness of the Dharma; third is mindfulness of the Saṃgha; fourth is mindfulness of generosity; fifth is mindfulness of the precepts; and sixth is mindfulness of the devas.

The first three are mindfulness of others, while the latter three are mindfulness of oneself. Generosity and the precepts are one's own causes, and the devas are one's own results. Furthermore, there are near and far results:
the near result is birth among the devas, and the far result is the ultimate deva (the *paramārtha-deva*). Moreover, the first three may also be considered forms of mindfulness of oneself.
"Self" refers to mindfulness of the Three Jewels as one essence. The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: "Mindfulness of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha is called the adornment of wisdom;

mindfulness of giving, precepts, and the heavens is called the adornment of merit. However, the practices cultivated above are intended for the swift attainment of the perfection of merit and wisdom, as well as the ten *pāramitās*, thereby suddenly transcending the mundane world and surpassing the three incalculable eons.

Kalpa. To pray for the swift attainment of the sacred fruit in this very life, one must resolve to attain Bodhicitta, exercise great compassion, and constantly desire to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, becoming equal to the Bodhisattva Cundī.

Furthermore, relying upon the boundless Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, may they provide empowerment, protection, and assistance through their great compassionate vows so that [this goal] is swiftly accomplished. Accordingly, one must rely on the aforementioned [method].
Select an excellent location to serve as the site for the mandala practice. Limit the duration to one period of four months and four days.
Only by severing all coming and going and speech can the three secrets be brought into correspondence. Face the east, which is the auspicious position, or alternatively, another direction.
If one is unable to construct the mandala according to the aforementioned ritual methods, there is another method that must also be followed.
Select a quiet place. Before a sacred image of Cundī, set up a clean mirror as an altar.
Facing the direction specified above, sit in the full lotus posture opposite the sacred image. The practitioner first visualizes the syllable *Lam* upon the crown of their own head.

It transforms into a triangular wheel of fire that, from the crown of the head down to the feet, completely incinerates one’s own body of outflows (*āsrava*) as well as this conditioned world (*saṃskṛta-loka*), just like the fire at the end of an eon (*kalpāgni*) which burns everything away until nothing remains but empty stillness.
Furthermore, one visualizes the syllable *Aṃ* at the aperture of one's crown; the very essence of this syllable is the Buddhas themselves.
The water of the Dharma of Radiance is used to sprinkle upon the crowns of the heads of the Buddha-sons; this is the secret empowerment dharma-gate.
Furthermore, visualize the establishment of the unconditioned mandala. At the very bottom, visualize the syllable *kham* in various colors pervading everywhere.
It becomes the wheel of space (*ākāśa-cakra*). Upon the wheel of space, one should visualize everywhere the black letter *haṃ*, which transforms into the wheel of wind (*vāyu-cakra*).
Upon the wheel of wind, one should visualize everywhere the red letter *laṃ*, which transforms into the wheel of fire (*tejas-cakra*).

Upon the wheel of fire, one should visualize everywhere the white letter *vaṃ*, which transforms into the wheel of water (*ap-cakra*). Upon the wheel of water, one should visualize everywhere the yellow letter *a*.
It transforms into a vajra-ground. Upon this vajra-ground, one should visualize a great lotus flower pervading everywhere.
Upon each flower, there is a Cundī Bodhisattva, making offerings with food, drink, banners, flags, and all other various articles of worship.
All of these face the mirror-altar of Cundī, with the three secrets in correspondence. Furthermore, if the practitioner lacks an image of Cundī, and...
With offerings such as flowers, fruits, and food, merely performing this visualization will bring about auspicious accomplishment.
Having formed this thought, one should single-mindedly and attentively contemplate the Bodhisattva Cundī, who is endowed with inexhaustible marks and signs and radiant light.
Within the moon disc at the Bodhisattva’s heart, there are nine sacred syllables arranged in a clockwise sequence. The practitioner should visualize the moon disc of their own heart.
Within the wheel, there are also nine syllables arranged as before. Upon one’s own body, from the crown of the head down to the feet, one likewise arranges nine syllables.
Next, recite the mantra for purifying the Dharma-realm, Oṃ-lam, and the mantra for protecting the body, Oṃ-ci-liṃ, twenty-one times each.
Thereafter, bind the root mudrā or the vajra-fist, and recite the Cundī mantra.
The mantra is indeterminate and beyond number. With single-minded devotion, one should diligently exert body and mind so as not to fall into indolence.
When the time for approaching accomplishment draws near, various obstacles may arise; one should subdue them by performing rites such as the *śāntika* (pacification) as described below.
Within a single lifetime, according to one's own spiritual capacity, one will certainly attain the manifestation of samādhi. Immediately upon...
Within meditative concentration, one sees innumerable Buddha assemblies and hears the sublime sound of the Dharma, thereby realizing the stage of a Bodhisattva of the Ten Grounds.

A practitioner who seeks accomplishment in this dharma must first perform a preliminary practice by reciting the Cundī mantra ten thousand times, or even up to one hundred thousand times. As stated in the Susiddhikara Sūtra: "If..."

If one does not first perform the recitation and mental retention to the point of complete pervasion, even the lower dharmas sought will not achieve accomplishment, let alone the higher or middling siddhis.
For this reason, one should cultivate a superior resolve and perform the preliminary recitation first.
Having performed these preliminaries, one may then see various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in dreams expelling black substances; this signifies the presence of transgressions.
This is the sign of the accomplishment arising from the extinction of merit. Just as you have prayed for what you seek, you shall certainly obtain the fulfillment of the result.

Do not give rise to a mind of doubt, nor entertain thoughts of acceptance or rejection. You must further exert yourself in the three karmas and increase your efforts in recitation and upholding [the mantra].
Furthermore, you must not flaunt this state of realization before others; it should be shared only with those of the same path, and never out of a desire for fame or profit.
Only after such praise may one proceed to explain it. Someone asked: "If one perceives signs as described above, will this not result in false and deluded attainment? He replied:

"Now, by relying on the sūtras to maintain the recitation and practicing correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), the sublime realm manifests spontaneously. This is not the same as other modes of cultivation which involve rejecting [the practice] or grasping at signs.
If one does not understand that each sūtra has its own specific intent, yet blindly conforms to others to harbor slander and destroy the Mahāyāna, one will sink into the mud oneself."

Plow. However, if a practitioner wishes to recite mantras, they must seek out an enlightened master who is well-versed in Sanskrit sounds and the methods of ritual practice, so as to receive instructions on the syllables, phrases, mudrās, and mantras without error; one must by no means follow one's own arbitrary mind.
If one recites without effect and conceives doubt toward the mantra, one invites misfortune upon oneself. The Susiddhi Sūtra states:

"Furthermore, if there is a person who has long practiced the recitation of a mantra of the lower grade, even if they lack personal power, they may seek it from the deity and attain the higher grade spontaneously.
However, if, regarding a mantra of the higher grade, one harbors hesitation in mind while reciting and maintaining it..."
If one makes offerings but lacks sincerity, or if the mind with which one recites even superior mantras is frivolous, it will result in only inferior accomplishment.
Thus, one should know that the efficacy of mantra recitation depends entirely upon the state of one's mind; by reciting with a sincere heart, one shall attain *siddhi*.
If a person recites a mantra for a long time without obtaining results, they must not abandon it, but rather redouble their vows and expand their aspirations.
One should increase one's diligence even further, making completion the limit. Such a person will swiftly attain accomplishment.
Within their dreams, or from the sky, a voice may speak, saying: "You should not hold this mantra-dharma, nor should you abandon it;
furthermore, do not feel anger toward it. Why? Because both are indeed Māras. You need only be diligent; you should not [be angry]."
One should refrain from retreating; let the mind not harbor evil thoughts; do not grasp at various objects or allow the sense faculties to run wild.
Constantly attain purity and perform recitation. Therefore, the *Gandharāja-dhāraṇī-sūtra* states: "Every day, filter water and bathe with fragrant water."

Wear separate garments. Whether walking or coming from afar, you must wash yourself clean in all matters, both large and small. When entering the altar, you must chew a *yācī* twig (*dantakāṣṭha*) before entering;
then, recite the mantra with a single mind, without thinking of external affairs. Regarding the method of holding the mantra:
one must not have a body that has violated the precepts, nor must one come into contact with a woman. If one does so touch her, there will be no efficacy.
Next, the four types of rites—pacification (*śāntika*), augmentation (*pauṣṭika*), subjugation (*vaśya*), and coercion (*abhicāra*)—are explained.
Regarding the rite of pacification (*śāntika*): it is for seeking the extinction of sins and the turning away of obstacles;

for removing calamities, malevolent spirits, diseases, imprisonment and shackles, pestilence, national crises, irregularities in water and drought, damage to crops by insects, and the oppression of the five planets upon one’s natal star.
All [afflictions] are completely eliminated and one is liberated from the defilements;
this is called the rite for pacifying calamities (*śāntika*). *Śāntika* is translated as "pacifying calamities," yet it also contains many other meanings;
therefore, the Sanskrit term is retained rather than being directly translated into Chinese. The three subsequent rites should be understood according to this principle.
When performing this rite, one should wear white garments, face north, and sit in the auspicious posture (bhadra-pīṭha) with the legs crossed and knees raised.
One should visualize the deity as white in color. All offerings—food, fruit, incense, flowers, lamps, and the ground—must likewise be entirely white.
Sitting with the legs crossed and the knees upright is called the *śrīvatsāsana* (Auspicious Seat). For fragrant ointments, use white sandalwood; for incense, use aloeswood (*agaru*);
for lamps, use clarified butter (*ghṛta*) as fuel. If clarified butter is unavailable, use white sesame oil. The original translation states: "Visualize it as being white. The Zhi translation states:
"Use white [substances] for all of them. The same applies to the three subsequent methods.
From the first day of the month until the eighth, recite the mantra three times each day and perform *homa* at night.
The mantra for pacifying calamities (*śānti*) is as follows: *Oṃ jale jale jvalini amukaṃ śāntiṃ kuru svāhā*. (If reciting for another, one should substitute that person’s name.)

*Vāhā*. (The commentary states: If one wishes to perform various methods such as *śāntika* (pacification), whether for oneself or for others, one may recite the mantra according to the prescribed rites.
If one desires to seek the pacification of calamities and the removal of all malevolent spirits, [one should do so].
O deity, for those who are wise, long-lived, and seek liberation, one should sit within the *maṇḍala* facing north with legs crossed and knees raised.
One should perform the recitation and *homa* rites three times daily.
When reciting, first recite the root *dhāraṇī* twenty-one times; thereafter, begin simply from the syllable *Oṃ*.
Recite it as follows: *Oṃ cili cili cundī svāhā*. [May this] remove the calamities and difficulties of such-and-such a person.
*Svāhā*. When performing this rite, one must do so within a ritual arena (*maṇḍala*); if no such arena is available, [one should perform it elsewhere].
Alternatively, one may arrange a mirror-mandala before an image of Cundī. Furthermore, one must visualize a white circular mandala;
within this circular mandala, one should visualize the syllable *vaṃ* or *praṃ* everywhere. Then, one should visualize the honored image, the ritual implements, and oneself [as being within it].
One should visualize [the deity] within a circular mandala; it is also permissible to simply smear a single circular mandala before an image.
With a mind imbued with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), beginning from the first watch of the night on the first day of the month until the eighth day, one should bathe three times each day.
Change one's clothes three times a day. When the period of days is complete, one may either fast or consume the "three white foods," namely:
milk, curd, and non-glutinous rice.
○ Regarding the *puṣṭika* rite: it is for seeking longevity, official rank and honor, hidden treasures, abundance, wisdom, and renown.

Maintain it without forgetting. The medicinal rites will be accomplished, as will the rites of the vajra and so forth. Alternatively, one may manifest the three signs—such as lions, elephants, or horses—through the empowerment of mantras.
One shall obtain the fruits sought according to whether they are superior, middling, or inferior, as explained in detail in the Susiddhikara Sūtra.
If one desires to seek the vidyādhara sages, one should enter the caves of the asuras, as well as the caves of the eight classes of spirits and deities.

Those who seek entry shall all attain it, as well as the stages of realization and supernormal powers. By seeking the perfection of the two types of provisions, one will swiftly achieve unsurpassed enlightenment;
this is called the method of augmentation. When performing this rite, one should wear yellow robes and face the east.
Sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). Visualize the deity as yellow in color. All offerings—incense, flowers, food, fruit, lamps, the ground, and so forth—are likewise entirely yellow.
For the unguent, use yellow sandalwood or white sandalwood with a small amount of saffron added. For the incense, use white sandalwood.
Light lamps of sesame oil.
From the eighth day of the month until the fifteenth, recite the mantra three times each day and perform *homa* at night. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ jyeṣṭhāyai jyeṣṭhānaye [name] puṣṭiṃ kuru svāhā. (The sound is *tshi*). The Wise One’s translation says:
If one wishes to seek the increase of the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), the turning of the wheel, and various treasuries of jewels.

Display the wheel, sword, auspicious flask (*bhadraghaṭa*), wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), *ānanda*, *yūlika* bell, battle-axe, noose, trident, and all other treasures and medicinal herbs. The seeker of accomplishment should wear yellow robes.
Continue the recitation as before. The sublime mantra says: Oṃ cili cili cinti.
Grant such-and-so [the name of the petitioner] their heart’s desire. Svāhā. If there is no ritual mandala, one may arrange a mirror-mandala before an image of Cundī.
Furthermore, visualize a square yellow mandala; within that square mandala, visualize the letter A everywhere.
The syllable *Aṃ* or the syllable *Haṃ*. Visualize the honored image, the ritual implements, and one’s own body together within a square mandala;
alternatively, it is also permissible to draw a square mandala in front of the image. Endowed with a mind of joy, perform the bathing and changing of clothes as previously described.
When the period is complete, it is also as previously described regarding fasting and so forth.

As for the manifestation of the three signs—namely, flames, smoke, and warmth—if a practitioner of mantras wishes to seek accomplishment, they should follow the various *dhāraṇī* sūtras and employ four types of objects:
first, a bow, arrow, battle-axe, hook, wheel, mallet, mirror, or alternatively, a rosary, flask, alms bowl, or monastic robe.
First, various items used by the Sangha, such as robes (*saṃghāṭī*) and so forth; second, various medicinal substances such as realgar and orpiment;

third, taking earth and mud from riverbanks to fashion the forms of various birds and beasts, such as lions, elephants, horses, oxen, camels, or chickens, geese, peacocks, and garuḍas; fourth, molding, painting, or carving [images].
Carve various images of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Vidyārājas according to one’s own inclination; having accomplished a single purpose through the ritual, place them within the maṇḍala.

Recite the mantra according to the rite, and when flames emerge, whether one holds them in the hand, smears them upon the body, or mounts them, one shall fly through the air together with one’s companions and spiritual friends. Or there may be...
If a person sees a siddha, or if a siddha sees such a person, they will both be able to ascend into the air and travel through all worlds, making offerings to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
their lifespan shall be one kalpa, and they will attain the first bhūmi and the gate of the hundred dharmas of illumination.
If smoke emerges, apply it as before; one will become a king among the various rishis and dwell for ten million years.
Year. If warmth emerges, one will gain the respect and affection of all humans and devas, and whatever is sought will be fulfilled as desired.
These are the signs of the three grades of accomplishment appearing. If a flame emerges, it is the sign of superior accomplishment.
If smoke emerges, it is the sign of middling accomplishment. If warmth emerges, it is the sign of inferior accomplishment. [In] the West...
In the past, there was a person who attained superior accomplishment and led five hundred people to ascend into the air.

It is further said that if the "fire-light" manifests, one will obtain the constant protection of all mantra-deities, and the assemblies of the eight classes of beings will always pay them respectful homage.

All divine mantras will yield the most supreme and efficacious results when employed. If the sign of smoke appears, wherever one goes there shall be no obstacles or difficulties, and all that is sought will be fulfilled according to one's heart’s desire.
If the sign of warmth appears, one will gain the sincere respect and affection of all people, as well as spirits and deities.
The Susiddhikara Sūtra states: "If one wishes to accomplish medicinal substances and the like..."
There are three types of accomplishment (*siddhi*). Blazing flames are the highest; smoke is the middle; and warmth is the lowest.
If one proceeds by traveling through space with mastery, this is the most excellent. Concealing one's form and hiding one's traces is the middle. Accomplishing various worldly affairs is the lowest.
These three types of accomplishment are further distinguished according to their superior, middling, and inferior degrees. This is the highest accomplishment.
Through this Dharma, one may become a Vidyādhara who travels through the air, achieve the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), or attain the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
One may attain the stage of a Pratyekabuddha, realize the level of a Bodhisattva, or gain knowledge and understanding of all matters.
One may acquire eloquence and great learning, or become a Vetāla, or a Yakṣiṇī, or attain the state of a Kinnara.
Or one may obtain the *dhāraṇīs*, or acquire inexhaustible treasures, and possess such superior matters as these; this is called the method for superior, middling, and inferior accomplishments.
If one conceals one's traces, one will attain great power within the body; one who was previously indolent will become diligent;

one will enter the palace of the Asuras and obtain the medicine of longevity; one will accomplish the *pātra-siṃha* (the lion-vessel) and become a celestial messenger (*devadūta*); or one will be able to command spirits. Or...
One can achieve mastery over the tree deity Śalabhañjika, or become widely learned and realize profound principles;
or one may compound medicines, or merely by anointing the feet and the crown of the head, travel great distances without any fatigue, as described above.

These are all termed methods for middling accomplishment (*madhyama-siddhi*). As for methods for inferior accomplishment (*adhamā-siddhi*), they cause the multitude to behold one with joy, or subjugate the masses, or are able to punish evil persons, subdue hostile hosts, and other such inferior matters;
these are termed methods for the lowest of the middling-inferior accomplishments (*adhamādhamā-siddhi*). If one sees a painted image, a *śarīra* stūpa, or the like suddenly shake, or emit light...

If flames emerge, you should know that accomplishment will be swiftly attained before long. The rest is as described in the aforementioned methods for recitation. Regarding the nine grades of the Dharma-light, from superior to inferior:

if one wishes to accomplish the Wheel-Rishi (*cakravartin*) rite, one should fashion a wheel from tempered steel (*vaidūrya-ayasa*), measuring two finger-widths and one span (*vitasti*) in circumference.
The wheel should have six spokes, with a rim and felloe that are sharp and keen. If one wishes to accomplish the Yellow Orpiment (*haritāla*) rite...
As for this: take the mineral pigment *haritāla* (yellow orpiment), which has a luster like the light emitted by the rising sun, or like the golden radiance of molten gold;

this is considered the finest quality. If one wishes to accomplish the rite of the sword (*khaḍga*), one should take a fine blade of *vimala* iron, measuring two cubits in length—equivalent to the span of the little finger—and four fingers in width, free from all defects, and blue-black in color like the plumage of the *kakkaṭaka* bird.

If one wishes to accomplish the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa* rite, one should fashion a *buddhoṣṇīṣa* out of gold, resembling a painted seal, and place it upon a pedestal. That pedestal should be supported by *sphaṭika* (crystal) gems.

If one wishes to accomplish the Lotus rite, one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus out of gold, measuring two finger-widths or one *vitasti* (span), or alternatively, one may fashion it out of silver. Or...

It may be made of refined copper or white sandalwood. If one wishes to accomplish the *vajra* rite, one should fashion a *vajra* from high-quality *bīṇī* iron, sixteen finger-widths in length, with three prongs at each end;
or it may be made of red sandalwood, gold, silver, or refined copper. If one wishes to accomplish the rite of realgar, one should take realgar that is the color of molten gold in solid lumps.
Analysis of components. Furthermore, there is light above. Thus, realgar can accomplish the aforementioned matters.
If one wishes to accomplish the rite of ox-gallstone (*gorocanā*), one should take the gallstone of a yellow cow as the best material.

If one wishes to accomplish the rite of the protective thread, one should take fine white woolen threads; three are joined together to form a strand, and three such strands are joined again to form the cord. [The cord is wound] by a young girl with her right hand...

Twist them together, or join them with gold thread. If one wishes to accomplish the purification of cow dung, take cow dung from a forest hermitage (*āraṇya*), burn it to ash, and mix it with *kakkola* (camphor) incense.

If one wishes to accomplish bows, arrows, spears, lances, single-pronged forks, clubs, and various other weapons for worldly use, one may fashion them as desired. If one wishes to accomplish a saddle...

Chariots drawn by horses, oxen, or sheep; all birds, beasts, and other such things—whatever the people of the world collectively regard as superior, whatever objects they fashion according to their own inclinations and desires, whether placed in vessels of gold, silver, refined copper, or conch shells.
Stone, wood, earthenware vessels, and the like; or spread with milk-leaves, incense-leaves, lotus-leaves, or plantain-leaves; or with fresh woolen cloth.
Take whatever is available and spread it out. Furthermore, using five layers of leaves, first spread them upon the ground and place the object to be accomplished thereon.
Then cover that object with another five layers of leaves—whether these be loose grains, various garments, or miscellaneous items—the sequence of which should be understood accordingly.
Afterward, using a vessel to hold these, perform the *tripuṭa* rite with an undistracted mind.

Illuminate the object with the light of the mind and sprinkle [the clarified butter] upon it. Holding a ladle in hand, slowly scoop up the *ghṛta* (clarified butter) and place it over the object while reciting the root mantra.
Upon reaching the syllable *svā*, pour it into the fire pit; upon reaching the syllable *hā*, touch the object again and return to the vessel containing the *ghṛta*.
In this manner, moving back and forth between these three points, one must touch the object without interruption. This is...
This is called the *Sampāta-homa* rite. During the *sampāta* [concluding] stage, one should use the ladle to sprinkle the substances everywhere, ensuring they are all thoroughly moistened.
When first placing the items, first sprinkle them with water, then press down upon them while reciting the mantra.
If the object to be accomplished is a sentient being, fashion its image; then, holding the ladle over its head, perform the *homa*. If one wishes to accomplish it for oneself, [use]...
Touch the tip of one's own head with the ladle; if performing it for another, simply call their name. Furthermore, there are three distinctions regarding the objects used for the homa:
first, merely calling the name; second, covering the object with something else as a barrier; third, leaving it exposed so that it is visible to the eye.
In all such cases, perform the homa using ghee (sarpis). If ghee is unavailable, one should use cow [milk].
Milk, or milk mixed with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), or the three sweets (*trimaṇḍaka*) should be used according to the specific distinctions of the accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Alternatively, one may sprinkle the object with scented water consecrated by reciting mantras, just as in the previously described method for manifesting the splendor of objects;
this case is also the same. Furthermore, the Susiddhikara-pūjā-vidhi states: "Among mantras, those containing the syllable *oṃ*... and so forth.
One should recite the *namas* (homage) syllable with a tranquil mind. If performing rites for pacification (*śāntika*) or enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), one should recite in a low voice.
If the mantra contains the syllable *hūṃ* or *phaṭ*, one should recite with fierce anger. Regarding the two kinds of provisions:
a bodhisattva who wishes to realize the fruit of Buddhahood must extensively cultivate the two dharmas of merit and wisdom as their foundation.
Only when the accumulations of merit and wisdom are perfected does one realize the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi. Now, for the practitioner who upholds mantras, there is no need for other practices;
by merely reciting according to the ritual method, one attains perfection and swiftly accomplishes unsurpassed Bodhi.

Regarding the ritual for *Vaśīkaraṇa* (subjugation): if one wishes to cause all people who see [the practitioner] to give rise to a heart of joy, and to attract, subdue, and summon—whether men or women, the eight classes of gods and nāgas, yakṣiṇīs, or even unruly spirits and ghosts;
or if there are enemies who perform harmful acts—one shall cause them all to turn their hearts toward joy. [This is the method of] the Buddhas.
This is the empowerment of protective mindfulness; it is called the rite for summoning and inspiring affection.
One who performs this rite shall wear red garments, face west, and sit with both knees raised and feet together, which is known as the "Noble Posture" (bhadrapīṭha).
There are briefly three ways of sitting: first, the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*); second, the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*); and third, the kneeling posture (*utkuṭukāsana*).
One should keep the body upright and motionless while performing the recitation.
Visualize the deity and all that is offered—incense, flowers, food, fruit, lamps, the ground, and so forth—as being entirely red in color.
For the unguent, use saffron; for the incense, burn cloves and storax mixed with honey. Then offer various fruits.
Using an oil lamp,
recite the mantra three times daily from the sixteenth to the twenty-third day, performing *homa* at night.
The mantra for summoning is as follows:
Oṃ cili cili cundī [insert name] vaśīkuru bhava ha. The translation says: If one wishes to summon all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and so forth, one should perform this rite.
... down to the sublime words: Oṃ cili cili cundī; for the purpose of summoning such-and-such a person.
Deity, fulfill my aspirations! Svāhā. ○ If there is no maṇḍala, one may arrange a mirror-maṇḍala before an image of Cundī.
Furthermore, one should visualize a red crescent-shaped maṇḍala; within this crescent maṇḍala, one should visualize the syllable *Ha* or *Haṃ* everywhere.
One should visualize that the honored image, the ritual implements, and one’s own body are all contained within the crescent.
Within the maṇḍala, or before the image, it is also permissible to smear only half a moon-shaped altar.
With compassion within and a wrathful appearance without, one should bathe and observe a fast as previously described.
Regarding the *ābhicāruka* rite: for those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution, who slander the Mahāyāna sūtras, who destroy the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*),

who rebel against their sovereign, or who cause confusion within the True Dharma— for such persons as these, one should give rise to profound compassion and perform the rite of subjugation (*abhicāra*).

If one performs this rite for the sake of seeking personal gain or against an enemy, according to the teachings of the various sūtras, it will certainly result in the opposite—invoking calamity and instead bringing about lifelong ignorance and folly. Therefore, the practitioner should exercise great caution.
Thus, the *Vajrapāṇi-cakra-vidhi-sūtra* states: "The mantra-practitioner must not allow their own mind to become deluded."
Out of hatred and envy, if one toward sentient beings who possess manifold virtues suddenly performs such an act for the purpose of causing them distress and harm,
they shall experience the resulting retribution by entering the Great Hell of Wailing (*Raurava*), where they will undergo manifold sufferings for immeasurable eons.
The mantra-practitioner must distance themselves from such faults and evils before they may practice this maṇḍala and seek various accomplishments.
One should smear the altar with donkey dung, camel dung, or the ashes of cremated corpses. When performing this rite, one should wear—
One should wear black robes or blue robes, face south, and sit in a squatting posture with the left foot pressing upon the right.
One visualizes the deity as black in color and offers flowers that are foul-smelling, odorless, black, or blue.
All offerings—including food, drink, incense, flowers, fruits, lamps, candles, and the ground—should likewise be black or blue.
"Press" (ō) means to suppress. Some say that for *argha* (offering water), a black vessel is used;
for food and drink, it is dyed black with pomegranate juice or made blue. For unguents (*vilepana*), cypress wood is used. For *argha*, cow urine is used.
Taking small portions of black flowers, mustard seeds, cypress wood, unguents, and so forth, place them into the *argha* water and burn *agallochum* (安息香).
Incense. Light a lamp of mustard oil. The *Vidyādharapiṭaka-vidhi* states:
Regarding the *argha* water, if performing a rite for pacification (*śāntika*), use milk and barley together; if performing a rite for enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), add sesame seeds;
if performing a rite for subjugation (*abhicāruka*), add blood and buckwheat. There are also distinctions regarding the *argha* vessels used. [The *Susiddhikara*...]
The *Dìjīng* (Earth Sūtra) states: Among soups and broths, those that are sweet in flavor, as well as milk porridge, are used for *śāntika* rites.
Those that are sour-sweet in flavor, as well as pomegranate porridge, curd porridge, and the like, are used for *pauṣṭika* rites.
Those that are bitter, pungent, or bland in flavor, as well as sesame, non-glutinous rice, beans, and so forth, are used for *ābhicāruka* rites, as previously described.
Various food flavors and the like may differ according to their respective locations; one should offer them while observing their superior, middling, or inferior qualities.
For all rites of fierce accomplishment (*tīkṣṇa-sādhana*) and *ābhicāruka* (subjugation), the times of solar and lunar eclipses are most appropriate.
The hearth should be triangular and smeared with one’s own blood, or [constructed] using *karkaṭaka* wood, or using [wood from] a burning [pyre].
Perform the homa using the remains of a corpse and firewood. Once the fire has been kindled, perform the homa by mixing the ashes from the cremation with one's own blood.
Furthermore, perform the homa by combining poisons with one's own blood and mustard oil mixed with red mustard seeds.
From the twenty-third day of the month until the end of the month, perform recitation during two periods—the midday and the midnight—and perform homa at night. The mantra is as follows:
HŪṂ. This is the homage; the homage is according to the rule. (For such-and-such a person), *prāṇaghātaya* HŪṂ PHAṬ.
The syllable HŪṂ is pronounced with the mouth closed, like the lowing of a cow. The syllable ṬHA is pronounced with half a sound. The Wisdom Translation states:
"If one wishes to subjugate all evil spirits and ghosts, as well as those who harm the Triple Gem among humans and devas, and who possess many sinful karmic obstructions..."

Regarding sentient beings who are heavy with afflictions and difficult to subdue, one should arouse compassion and perform this rite so as to cause them to generate the bodhicitta and cultivate various virtuous deeds, and so forth. The Susiddhikara Sūtra states: "There may be certain mantras..."
If at the beginning there is the syllable *go* and at the end there is the syllable *ṭha*, one will swiftly achieve accomplishment in the *ābhicāruka* rite.

Furthermore, one must be well-versed in the methods for practicing mantra. According to the specific objective sought, one should recite the mantra that corresponds to the characteristics of that particular rite;

by doing so, accomplishment will be attained. The *Vidyādharapiṭaka* states: "When performing rites of pacification (*śāntika*) or enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), one should softly recite the syllable *HŪṂ* and the syllable *PHAṬ*. When performing rites of subjugation (*abhicāruka*), one should arouse wrath."
With a wrathful mind, recite the syllables *HŪṂ* and *PHAṬ* with a stern voice.
○ If there is no maṇḍala, one may arrange a mirror-maṇḍala before an image of Cundī. Furthermore, visualize a blue triangular maṇḍala;
within this triangular maṇḍala, visualize the syllable *RA* or *LAṂ* everywhere. Visualize that the honored image, the ritual implements, and one’s own body are all present therein.
Within a triangular mandala, or before an image—where it is also sufficient to merely smear a single triangular mandala—one should correspond with a wrathful mind.
Having bathed, changed clothes, and fasted as previously described, if wicked persons and others become uneasy in body and mind, [the rite shall proceed].
If someone contracts a serious illness, or if their life is about to end, one should immediately exhort them to give rise to a virtuous mind.
If they repent, reproach themselves, and forever sever their evil intentions, one should perform the recitation of the *śāntika* (peaceful) rite for that person;
the person will then be spared from calamity. If one wishes to seek accomplishment within these four aforementioned methods, one must...
First, as a preliminary practice, one should recite the Cundī Dhāraṇī five hundred thousand times, seven hundred thousand times, or one million times.
Only after this may one perform whichever of the four methods suits one’s inclination; success will then be certain.
One should follow the root sūtra in employing the mantras and mudrās to demarcate the boundary (*sīmābandha*), protect the body, and perform the offerings and invitation.

Invoke the deity. Upon completing the recitation, again perform the offerings, the dissolution of the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*), and the ritual dismissal of the deity and other deities using their respective mudrās and mantras.
Therefore, the *Vidyādharapiṭaka Sūtra* states: "If one performs the four aforementioned rites, one must necessarily invoke the deity and the assembly of worthy sages;
once the ritual is completed, one must then dismiss them. The *Susiddhikara Sūtra* states: "When the homa is finished..."
Having done so, use the mantra of the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) to consecrate pure water with the mantra; sprinkle it from a distance into the hearth in this manner three times.
When the *homa* is entirely completed, and after further performing offerings and so forth, dismiss [the deities] according to the ritual rules.
Furthermore, a practitioner of the *mantra* path should not engage in mutual testing with another practitioner who holds a different recitation.
If there is a minor transgression, one should not perform rites of subjugation (*abhicāra*). The *Vidyādharapiṭaka* states:
"Moreover, the practitioner shall take thread dyed with red flowers, have it spun by a young girl, empower it one thousand times with the *mantra*, and tie seven knots."
Having done so, tie it at the side of the waist. The mantra is: Oṃ hara hara patti śukra dhāri vi siddhi svāhā. (Note: *śu* may also be written as *sū*).
This mantra is also capable of subduing Śukra and destroying Śatru. Susiddhi.
The *Dhāraṇī-sūtra* states: Take white woolen thread or hemp fibers, have a young girl dye them red or saffron-colored (*kumkuma*), and form a cord by tying knots.
Recite the mantra seven times for each knot; do this for each one until there are seven knots. Place it before the deity and recite the mantra one thousand times over it.
When reciting mantras, when performing homa, or when about to lie down to sleep, one should fasten [the cord] around the waist so as not to lose seminal impurity.
When lying down, one should do so like a lion king, lying on the right side. The mantra is the same as above, with the exception that the word *pūrṇa* is used;
thus, it becomes *pūrṇa pūrṇa*. Furthermore, the Susiddhi Sūtra’s method for making offerings states: "As for its waist..."
Regarding the thread: have a young girl twist it together clockwise; after three twists, twist it again three times.
If it is made from *netra-tūla* (cotton) or *karpāsa* (cotton), sprinkle it with the five purifiers (*pañcagavya*). The mantra for the five purifiers of the Buddha Family is as follows:
*Namo bhagavate uṣṇīṣāya viśodhaya virājite svāhā*. Furthermore, it is said:

having accomplished the rite according to the previous method using flowers dyed with red madder or saffron, one should recite the mantra for binding the cord one thousand times during the recitation.
When performing *homa* or when sleeping, one should tie it around the waist; this will prevent the loss of semen.
During the time of recitation (*japa*) and during *homa*, one must wear the upper garment with the right shoulder bared. When defecating or urinating, one should wear wooden sandals (*kiri*).
One must not wear them in the presence of the tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), the two teachers, or senior elders. To speak slander against the Vaipulya [sūtras]...

The Mahāyāna refers to the various great sūtras such as the Avataṃsaka, the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka, the Śūraṅgama, the Laṅkāvatāra, the Vimalakīrti, the Samantabhadra-bodhicitta-uttaratantra (or Yuanjue), the Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda, and the Mahāparinirvāṇa.

These scriptures extensively discourse upon *tathatā* and the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), asserting that all sentient beings have been fundamentally enlightened from the beginning and that their nature inherently possesses virtues and functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
To slander and disbelieve these teachings is to harm both oneself and others, leading both to fall into the Avīci hell.
Even if a thousand Buddhas were to appear in the world, none could rescue those who destroy their Buddha-nature.
This refers to all sentient beings, who inherently possess Buddha-nature; yet, due to the accumulation of delusive thoughts and afflictions, they fail to realize it.

If one ceases delusion and returns to the truth, one immediately shares the same source of awakening as all Buddhas. However, ordinary people hold false views, disparaging and disbelieving this, both for themselves and others.
They sever the seeds of the Buddha-nature and become icchantikas, who are difficult to save for kalpas on end;
therefore, one generates deep compassion for such persons, performs rites of subjugation, and causes them to turn their minds toward the good. The *Vidyādharapiṭaka* states:
"If that which begins with the syllable Oṃ is employed, one can accomplish all dharmas; if [it begins with] the syllable Ja..."
The three methods of pacifying, increasing, and subjugating possess great power.
The syllable *Ḍe* can destroy *śatrus*, as well as perform rites of expulsion and protection; its efficacy is supreme. The syllable *Ma* can effect destruction.
And it scatters the armies of others, just as the garuḍa is able to devour dragons. The syllable *li* destroys all great evils and possesses supreme power.
The syllable *tsun* (*tsnu*) accomplishes everything and can break even firm fetters.

*Appendix: Essential Points for Recitation*

This essential teaching is intended primarily for beginners who, while practicing according to the sutras, have not yet purified their three karmas and are thus unable to perform various contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā*).
Nevertheless, upon hearing of the extraordinary merit of this *dhāraṇī*, they may feel an urgent desire to recite it.
Alternatively, those of dull faculties, upon hearing of the sutra’s mantras and contemplative practices, may give rise to fear and retreat, thereby losing the sprout of the Bodhi-dharma.
It possesses immeasurable merit, as described in the sūtras. If a person recites it even once, the sprout of the dharma of bodhi immediately arises;
how much more so for those who can constantly recite, contemplate, and uphold it? Through these roots of goodness, one swiftly becomes a seed of Buddhahood and achieves all immeasurable merits.
Thus, the Vidyādhara-piṭaka states: "If there are sentient beings who commit great evil deeds and possess no goodness..."
For such a person, the seed of bodhicitta has no means of arising, and the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) will never be attained.

Yet, if such a person should suddenly encounter a spiritual friend who recites this mantra, and it but once passes through their faculty of hearing, their heavy sins will be diminished and the seeds of virtue will immediately sprout;
how much more so if they constantly maintain the recitation with focused diligence! As the Maṇḍala Commentary states: "Reciting the name of the Tathāgata..."
This divine mantra is a secret resonance between mind and mind with the Tathāgata’s mind; it is the recitation of the Bodhisattva’s secret words.
May every aspiration be in dark harmony with the Bodhisattva’s vows. What birth-and-death is there from which one cannot escape? What nirvāṇa is there that cannot be attained?

Because such benefits exist, this essential dharma has been compiled for the sake of easy reception and retention. If a practitioner wishes to recite it, they must first eliminate all external conditions.

Arousing a mind of profound reverence and conceiving the thought that such an encounter is difficult to find, go before a sacred image or face a mirror-altar. Stand upright and perform the gesture of joining the palms in prostration;
